items.title: Linklater's film Slacker (1991): Radical and Mediocre
items.text:
# On this fine day in Austin, TX, I got Linklater'ed.

It doesn't happen often, but I can count on it when Linklater made it. Can I even describe it? It's like this: you see a film, and then you live in that world for the rest of the day. You found it so comfortable and novel there, that reality colors your vision for a while, a constructed reality, sure (and eventually you'll settle back into what you know as reality, because it is unnatural for reality to bend into one shape for too long).

I've seen several Linklater films, most notably the *Before* trilogy and *Boyhood*. So when I heard a film enthusiast describe *Slacker*, I knew it would be the kind of thing I'd take to, no problem. Plus, filmed in the city I live in more than 30 years ago, I was looking forward to spotting familiar landmarks and marveling at landscape changes. And that is part of the experience I really enjoyed, but then another part of my mind has been captured by the film, and I am unable now to steer it away, so I've come here to write about it.

That's the thing with Linklater, I find. You don't just casually see these films. There's an incubation period once it's over. It's integrating itself into you. There's a heavy dose of culturally-relevant mind-melding technology in whatever he's doing with the pictures on the screen, the characters on display. Today I found out how hungry I have been for this kind of entertainment.

## about the film

> [*Slacker*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slacker_(film)) follows a single day in the life of an ensemble of mostly under-30 [bohemians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohemianism "Bohemianism") and misfits in [Austin, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas"). The film follows various eccentric and misfit characters and scenes, never staying with one character or conversation for more than a few minutes before moving on to someone else in the scene and following them.

![](https://m.stacker.news/167045)
^ that's Rick kicking off the whole thing with talk of strange dreams

> The characters include a talkative taxi passenger (played by Linklater), a [UFO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unidentified_flying_object "Unidentified flying object") [buff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fan_(aficionado) "Fan (aficionado)") who insists the U.S. has been on the [moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon") since the 1950s, a [JFK conspiracy theorist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_assassination_conspiracy_theories "John F. Kennedy assassination conspiracy theories"), an elderly [anarchist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarchy "Anarchy") who befriends a man trying to rob his house, a [television set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_set "Television set") [collector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collecting "Collecting"), and a woman trying to sell a [Madonna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madonna_(entertainer) "Madonna (entertainer)") [pap smear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pap_test "Pap test").

![](https://m.stacker.news/167049)

> Other characters include a woman hiding a black eye behind sunglasses who offers a random pick of [Oblique Strategies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oblique_Strategies "Oblique Strategies") to passers-by, a young man who perhaps accidentally or perhaps intentionally has run over his mother with the family car, three renters in a rooming house who discover and read a pack of postcards on the floor of a fellow renter who has moved out, a young woman who has just arrived back in town after her parents put her in a mental hospital in [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas"), and a man who tries to convince a friend to throw a tent and a typewriter into a creek to reject an ex-girlfriend symbolically.

![](https://m.stacker.news/167050)

![](https://m.stacker.news/167051)

## on being bohemian

I'm responding to the film because I'm identifying with it, and I'm nostalgic for it. The perfect cocktail for a lingering rumination of conceivable significance. I'll be nursing my headache in the morning.

See, I'm a collector, right? And my favorite objects are characters, people who've got something to say, something you could never anticipate, predict, or expect. When I've been passive observer of the grungy art and music scene, I find it as thrilling as riding a rollercoaster. And there have been periods of my life where I've gotten to live out a type of bohemian fantasy, like where people aren't really people, but characters. Each one offering me an interesting scrap that I'll capture in some way. And Linklater made a movie out of this pastime.

But where are these characters now? I can't find them in Austin in 2026. Now, you catch up with your buddy's band passing through to play a show, and all the bandmates scatter across east Austin searching for and finding drugs. And you follow them to make sure nothing bad happens, and they just wanna eat, and they don't say anything interesting. Or you throw a house party for the first time in ages and people stand around discussing ROI and you get so depressed by that. Or you go to an art show opening and no one is relaxed enough to even look you in the eyes, the room's so stuffed with self-importance. Or you made too many jokes poking fun at gay people and now your friends won't invite you out to see their gay plays which you find out later are really sucky anyway. I don't know, I ramble on. I'm just complaining because I miss freaks.

I miss the sensation of standing in front of a stranger and having no clue what might come out of their mouth. That sensation is the main character of *Slacker*.

## what is radical is mediocre

Turning to a different observation of the film, now that my personal confession is out of the way, there's a funny irony in the sincerity of this character's passionate convictions and the fact that their all slackers. For example, the climactic moment that a gun is pulled out in a robbery, the tension it introduces is immediately dissolved by the friendly banter of an aging man. The robber went in with the gun, right, but couldn't commit himself to the use of it, so he takes the cup of coffee offered to him. It's a little silly. It's a special silliness that belongs to sincere people who over-identify themselves with a political idea. And that happens to be a lot of bohemians, or leftists as we now know them. But that term doesn't capture the misfits, the unpopular weirdos pursuing uncomfortable hobbies, the harmless conspiracy-theorists, those who believe in something radical but live sheltered in mediocrity. Is that an expressly American thing? And did these people stop existing recently when they found out their uniqueness, nothing more, could be made profitable online?

I wonder about that, and a few other things.

Ah, another thing I loved about this film, not a drop of makeup anywhere to be seen.

items.title: Austin trip day two: I ask to pay with bitcoin and someone tried to choke me
items.text:
Hey stackers,

Writing from the poker room after a four hour session. Taking a long break before I head back. Here’s my favorite hand from the sesh if you’re interested:

https://stacker.news/items/1603097/r/SatAttack?commentId=1603670

I woke up later than I wanted to knocking on my hotel door. It was 930 and housekeeping wanted to clean my room. I politely declined, got out of bed, brushed my teeth and quickly made my way out. There were things to see and bitcoin to spend. @plebpoet had recommended Caffe Medici as a place you can buy coffee and pastries for sats so that’s where I went first. There’s three locations and with some poking around I found the origional one. It’s in a nice quiet part of town and the ambience from outside looked really cool.

Here’s their BTCmap: [https://btcmap.org/merchant/way:382559089](https://btcmap.org/merchant/way:382559089)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163624)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163625)

I loved these stone chairs and tables. I wish I could have captured them all but some were being used and I didn’t want to take pictures of strangers. Inside was really nice too. Lots of plants and plenty of seating. I head to the counter where I see their square terminal and order a red eye which if you don’t know is an espresso shot with a regular coffee poured over it. It will clear the mind and wake up the bowels. Good for the morning. Right in the middle of asking if she would accept bitcoin she rings me up and answers my question; I see that wonderful toggle in the top left of some square terminals. I toggle to Bitcoin and I’m presented with a lightning address. I pay it with Phoenix no issues.

I asked her how often people pay with bitcoin—not very often, I guessed. She said only some times. She had been working there for four months and I was the third person to pay with sats. Not bad actually, I thought. It’s not like she rings everyone up, so there could have been others.

After a few sips of coffee and a couple pages from the second book of the Outlander series by Diana Gabaldon, I realized I had forgotten to check the parties! Fool boy. I asked where they came from, I don’t remember the name, but they get them from a local bakery here in Austin. I ended up with a blueberry muffin and toggled over to Bitcoin and sent another successful transaction.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163627)

![](https://m.stacker.news/163628)

I had plans to go to jiujitsu at the Austin 10th planet at 11 but waking up late was really deterring me from executing that plan. I really wanted to skip the workout and stay on this couch with my book and coffee. I read and read some more and checked the time. It was 1030. The gym was only 15 min away. There was time to not skip…. Over to my left I notice they have whole beans for sale on the shelf and decide there. I’ll
Buy some beans and stop being lazy. After the third lightning transaction in the last hour she tells me you get a free coffee with a bag of beans purchase….. UuuUgh it really sounded nice to sit and read with my free cup. Instead I take it to go and head to the gym.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163629)

I arrive at the gym 10 minutes before class time. I didnt bring a rash guard so I needed to buy one and told the guy over the counter as much. I asked if I could pay for both with bitcoin and he was a bit hesitant. “I think so” he said. He’s showing me the options for rash guards that are hanging on the racks when I see a box on the floor with some orange and black material inside. The box is labeled “b-coin”

Are these rash guards?! I ask
Oh yeah, they are. You want one of those?
Uuuuh YEAH. He pulls one out and shows it to me and it’s AWESOME. Here it is on me:

![](https://m.stacker.news/163630)

He had to text the owner and inquire about my bitcoin request. She responded pretty quickly and texted him a QR code made by cash app. The ones that you can pay either lightning or on-chain to. I took the opportunity to save some liquidity from my Phoenix channel and paid on-chain with Blue Wallet. I told him he should let her know I made an on-chain payment and that I was confident she’d be ok with that. And that she should receive the payment in about ten minutes. I paid 3sats/vB to ensure that was accurate.

Equipped with my new sweet rash guard it was time to start class. Everyone was very welcoming in introductions and we got to work pretty quickly. We warmed up with some bridges and shrimps and got right into the lesson. Today we were going to work on getting a hip toss from full guard and failing the attempt some attacks you can do instead.

My partner was great, I wish I remembered his name. I’m fairly novice, and he was patient and helped me with some important details on the attacks we were learning. We went over locking the Americana after the failed hip toss, then the guillotine, the triangle, the kimura, and omaplata all stemming from the original hip sweep attempt from full guard. during practice  I took a nasty elbow to the lip that swelled right away and filled my mouth with an iron taste (wear a mouthguard kids). Lesson complete, the next hour was open mat. They started the 5 min repeat clock and let people get sparring rounds in. I did a couple before hit hitting the showers. I’m a bit out of jiujitsu shape haha. Awesome stuff. Awesome class. Thanks coach Curtis!

![](https://m.stacker.news/163631)

On my way out the gym coach Curtis was at the front desk. I had asked him earlier for this group picture and told him I will
Blog about my day today on a forum. “Blog or vlog?” He asked.

Blog.

“People still read?” Haha YES I told him. And I told him where I’d blog as well I told him about stacker news and what it’s like. I told him the idea that because valuable things are used to express like-ness valuable content surfaces to the top. I showed him my stacker news and made a couple zaps. He was really intrigued. “A negligible amount I assume, like a small amount of sats?” Ummmm YES SIR. I was happy to hear him use the word sats. Bitcoin was normal for him, it seemed. He said he will check it out and that seemed like the perfect opportunity to give him one of the SN stickers @k00b gave me yesterday. He loved the sticker and joked about putting it up on the stall door so people were forced to see it. I’m sure he was joking but I really hope that happens. Then he asked me if I was the guy who paid with bitcoin today. I said yes and he goes “ok let me hook you up” (!!!)

He said anyone repping and using bitcoin he wants to help out. Wow… awesome. He starts digging around in the “b-coin” bin looking for a pair of shorts to give me. They didn’t have my size, unfortunately, and so he offered a long sleeve rash guard instead. I had to decline. I have many rash guards back at home and I didn’t want to take one just because it was free. He told me I can come back to the gym for free while I was on my trip… I was so grateful. How cool! He showed me around the gyms grocery store which was actually rather stocked. They had grass fed beef. They order by the cow and sell frozen beef from the gym. They had raw milks and other treats. Loaves of bread. All sorts of locally made goods. He told me the raw milks were made by a lady who loves bitcoin and sometimes they use Bitcoin to transact with her. Hooter Flats was the name of her company. I bought one of the chocolate milks. Perfect post-training snack.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163632)

Workout complete I wanted to head to play some poker but I needed to eat first. I pretty quickly decided to head back to the Green Mestique from yesterday and get the same thing but different meats. I ordered the turkey, chopped beef, and the sausage. I had to get that sausage again. For sides I got potato salad and repeated the green beans as well. When they brought my plate they had given me chicken  instead of the turkey. No matter, I knew it was great. I couldn’t resist putting the BBQ sauce all over the chicken even though it stung like hell the cut on my inner lip. But I worked through the tears and finished strong.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163634)

And that’s day two! I went to the poker room after this and I am just now starting another session. I’ll probably play a couple hours before heading to bed.

If you missed my day one report check it out here: https://stacker.news/items/1602995/r/SatAttack

See you stackers, thanks for reading.

items.title: Nathan Pinkoski's Introduction to "The Camp of the Saints" by Jean Raspail
items.text:
If you've never heard of the book *The Camp of the Saints*, you're not alone.  Widely maligned as a racist screed, it's a 1973 dystopian novel by award-winning French author Jean Raspail that tells the tale of an armada transporting a million migrants from India to the shores of France, throwing the country into social chaos.  The novel predicts, almost a tee, the modern reactions and counter-reactions to mass migration in Western Europe and America.  Because of its unflattering depiction of immigrants and the consequences of mass migration, its print run in English was limited, and it wasn't until recently that a revised English translation became widely available.

I heard of the book through my watching of videos by Raymond Ibrahim, another person often maligned as racist and Islamophobic.  By revealing the kinds of people I watch and the kinds of books I read, I suppose I am outing myself as a potential bigot, but in my defense I'll offer that I read books [critical of Western imperialism](https://stacker.news/items/1405134) as well.

I decided to pick up the 2025 English translation by Vauban books, which contains a nice introduction by Nathan Pinkoski, an American conservative intellectual.  I was so impressed by the introduction that I decided to post selected excerpts from it here for stackers to read.    Hope it triggers some interesting discussion and some interest in the book.

`<begin Pinkoski>`

***

## Introduction

You are holding in your hands one of the most important dystopian novels ever written.

But unlike Aldous Huxley’s Brave New World and George Orwell’s 1984, Jean Raspail’s The Camp of the Saints lacks any aura of respectability. In the United States, it is attacked as a bigoted screed, “a must-read within white supremacist circles.” Raspail, who won some of France’s most important literary prizes, is regarded as an outright racist rather than as an accomplished writer. This narrative has stood for years in large part because the publishing houses that owned the rights to the English translation have suppressed the book. That is why the authorized release of this new edition by Robert Laffont, the French publishing house that owns the original rights, is so important. For the first time in many years, English-speakers have unrestricted access to the text, brought to life in Ethan Rundell’s vivid new translation. English-language audiences can now finally understand Raspail’s hypnotic and haunting tale and appreciate why the novel remains of lasting significance.

Huxley’s Brave New World and Orwell’s 1984 show how the assumptions of self-satisfied materialism, far from building a progressive paradise, can underwrite a permanent political nightmare. Describing fully achieved dystopias, the novels capture two sides of modern despotism: one, soft and seductive; the other, hard and brutal. The Camp of the Saints, by contrast, divulges a dystopia as it comes to be. It explores the implications of modern spiritual self-hatred.

The central plot concerns an armada that transports a million migrants from India to the shores of France, throwing the country and the West into chaos. But The Camp of the Saints is not a disaster novel. The book’s importance does not hinge on whether Raspail was correct in predicting mass immigration or in describing it in catastrophic terms. Rather, the novel’s genius lies in the depiction of an apocalypse in the original sense of that term. Properly translated, apocalypse means revelation, disclosure – literally, an “uncovering.” The Camp of the Saints, whose title is taken from the Book of Revelation, unveils the perverse logic that pervades late Western civilization, throwing into sharp relief the nihilism of guilt. Too spiritually weak to appreciate their own distinction and to defend themselves, Westerners welcome their own destruction under the guise of creating a perfect world cleansed of their past sins.

When interpreted by careless critics – and they are legion – The Camp of the Saints is about a fictional race war, a device for stoking fears about genocide against whites. This is the standard reading of both racialists and progressives. But for decades, thoughtful people could discuss other interpretations. National Review and The Atlantic published sober, sympathetic essays on The Camp of the Saints by distinguished scholars.4 Those days are gone. There’s little hope that those steeped in progressive lore will take this novel seriously. And many American conservatives now enforce the rules of reading set by the Left. Even in the few remaining institutions they control, conservatives are constantly fearful of progressive reproaches. In their quixotic bids to charm the same leftists who hate them, conservatives purge their ranks and turn on their friends. The reader of this book should be warned: to talk about The Camp of the Saints, still less to take it seriously and defend it, is not for the faint of heart. You must be prepared to pay the price.

Those who are anxious about The Camp of the Saints fixate on passages in which Raspail describes the migrants as primitive and barbaric; they see this as evidence that the book is a white supremacist tract. But this reading misses the point of the novel. Raspail is holding a mirror up to Western society: he is concerned with “us,” not “them.” Moreover, the attempt to slander Raspail and his work as the incarnation of white supremacy betrays a profound ignorance of Raspail’s life and vocation as the literary voice of the world’s forgotten peoples.

## Biography

\[*Here, Pinkoski gives a biography of Raspail, primarily to show that he most certainly was NOT racist by any means, but rather admired cultures different from his own.  Raspail's purpose in writing The Camp of the Saints was to explore whether Europe could lose its culture like other cultures before it.  Here are selected excerpts from the biography*]

...

The journey clarified Raspail’s vocation. Discovering an abandoned Algonquin village on an island in Lake Huron, Raspail received one of the decisive shocks of his life. “I remember my emotion,” he wrote, “as if I entered into a church and rediscovered my faith.” An awe for the world’s almost-vanished tribes guided him thereafter. The crew spent the night in the middle of the village, though without raising their flag – guests of the place’s original occupants, not conquerors. Later on during their journey, Raspail met a man, “Bill,” who chided him and his friends for their naïve Indianisme. “In Europe,” he told them, “dreams of the past take up too much place in your life. Here, we don’t talk of the past, but of the dam and the hydroelectric plant.” Raspail’s whole literary career could be described as a revolt against this attitude. Countering those who spurn the past and hail technological conformity, Raspail told the stories of disappearing peoples whom progressives consigned to extinction.

...

Raspail’s best novels are an unusual kind of historical fiction. They encompass historical events that veer off into the realm of fantasy, of historical counterfactuals that recount the sudden resurfacing of long-lost dynasties or peoples. L’Anneau du pêcheur (The Ring of the Fisherman) envisages the resurgent lineage of the Avignon papacy. Qui se souvient des hommes … (Who will remember the people …), portrays the Alakalufs; on the cusp of extinction, their language has no word for happiness, but hundreds to express suffering. Pêcheur de lunes (Fisher of Moons) depicts the remnants of the Ainu of Northern Japan and Russia. Sire, a kind of theological thriller, imagines a king of France crowned in contemporary Europe, as the regalia of the lost Arthurian world reemerge. Like other twentieth-century European writers, Raspail enjoyed mixing real and fictitious places, often gesturing toward the old, vanishing Europe. Hergé created a new monarchy in the Balkans, Syldavia, for Tintin to explore. It harkened back to the ancient monarchies of pre-1914 Europe. Raspail imagined a new Central European principality, Altheim-Neufra. It also harkened back to the stabilities of aristocratic Europe, lost after the world wars.

Two themes pervade Raspail’s work. One is a literary royalism. Raspail offers up monarchy not as a readily applicable political program, but rather as a transcendent, poetic refuge from the banality of modern politics. It captures at once a regret for what is lost, a defiance of the follies of the present, and a dream for what may come. The other theme is love for places and peoples distant in time and space. This love shapes Raspail’s determination to transmit the memory of almost vanished nations. Sometimes it led him to deliver particularly harsh tirades against the present. Modern New York, he judged, was “a desert” because “we no longer run into an Algonquin.”14 Chanting this polyphonic hymn to the nobility and fragility of the world’s peoples, Raspail affirms the particularity of cultures and civilizations. There’s no agenda in him for imposing Western norms across the globe. The world cannot be refitted into the model of the “dam and the hydroelectric plant.” Had Raspail kept his study of indigenous tribes to the far-off places unfamiliar to most Westerners, he might have preserved an unblemished reputation as a novelist and writer with arguably anti-colonialist sympathies.

Yet in one early work, he committed an unpardonable offense. He wondered whether the fate of the indigenous peoples of Europe would be similar to the peoples who had vanished in the wake of European colonization. Now, as Europeans retreated from their empires, were they just as vulnerable, just as liable to vanish from history – and just as deserving of a lament? Sometime in the 1960s and 70s, such thinking became taboo. And so for better or for worse, all of Raspail’s literary oeuvre is now measured by the one novel that took up those questions and imagined the end of European and Western civilization.

## The Novel

\[*Here, Pinkoski offers his analysis of the novel. It is full of spoilers, so I will only post some spoiler-free excerpts here*.]

...

The ethic of decolonization trades off the utopian vision of multicultural progressivism, which assumes that everyone in the world can be incorporated into a single rainbow regime. Yet the universalism underlying this project masks its coercive, dystopic dimension. Raspail pulls aside the mask. Multicultural progressivism demands the subjugation and destruction of all traditional forms of life. Its prime target is the West because the engine that drives it is Western cowardice and self-hatred; multiculturalism is the cultural imperialism of European self-loathing. Such impulses are masked by belief in the atoning power of capitulation to mass immigration and the deconstruction of European identity. But Raspail knows the truth: immigrants do not have the power to deliver Europeans from their sense of worthlessness. Once one embraces the logic of civilizational repudiation, the endpoint is nihilism and cultural death. The Alpha is European guilt. The Omega is Eurocide.

The plot of The Camp of the Saints is fantasy, but it is not frivolous. By the 1980s, those able to perceive the trajectory of European and French society saw that the novel could not be dismissed. Mitterrand thanked Raspail for sending him the book, which he promised to read “with much interest.” Jospin thanked Raspail for writing the book, “which describes a future that is not,” which is to say: a future that was in the process of happening. As the shadow of political correctness descended upon French intellectual life, leftists who could never praise the book in public did so in private. In 2004, Denis Olivennes, who managed the French left-wing daily Libération, wrote to Raspail: “Thirty years ago, I would have undoubtedly considered The Camp of the Saints as a despicable polemic.” But since reading it, “not only do I no longer hate those who do not think like me, I’m interested in them!” Robert Badinter, the Jewish socialist Minister of Justice, a champion of international human rights law who abolished the death penalty in France, thanked Raspail for the 1985 edition. “Ten years ago I read it with great interest,” he wrote. “With the flow of time the problem has become more pressing … The civilization which is ours is only threatened from the inside, more by losing its soul than by yielding to external demographic pressures.”

Badinter discerned that we are imperiled above all by Western civilization’s own internal spiritual crisis. This insight is what now makes The Camp of the Saints so disturbing to read. The desire to make ourselves culturally prostrate has come into the open.

...

Raspail was concerned to do more than unveil that spiritual death of the West. The Camp of the Saints offers guidance to those of us who hope to save our spiritual integrity as we seek to preserve and honor our patrimony. It shows us how not to act. The novel’s band of resisters, though patriots who love their country and culture, are very much part of Raspail’s satire. At best, they practice a simple postwar Epicureanism, appreciating the quotidian pleasures afforded by their country’s prosperity, customs, and culinary traditions. At worst, they lack ethical refinement and display a rough, schoolboy Nietzscheanism. They are lovers of sensual pleasures but they are also lovers of violence. They have only the fragments of the real religion. They are Last Men.

The tragic center of the novel is a civilization pulled between two portals of death. On the one hand, there is an eschatological universalism, premised on the unique guilt of one civilization, which makes the collective suicide of the West a spiritual duty. On the other hand, there is a raw particularism, which may animate the community, but leaves its members bereft of pity and mercy and so devoid of any authentic spirituality. For Christians, the novel poses a dilemma. Either uphold a natural love of home and country and reject Christianity; or uphold Christianity but reject the natural love of home and country.

...

We in the West are in thrall to a false dilemma between universalism and particularism. It may be the specific charism of French Catholicism to overcome it. This is a charism that can heal a world where the old Christian virtues have gone mad, guiding the Church to recover the fullness of her treasures and helping the baptized nations of the West save their souls.

Whatever the ultimate theological resolution may be, Raspail’s later works are literary explorations that take us beyond the novel’s dilemma. Just like The Camp of the Saints, these are novels about cultural destruction that imagine what survivors and resisters must do after the catastrophe has occurred. Just like The Camp of the Saints, they describe little platoons of resisters who try to save a culture threatened with extinction, to protect the fragile roots of traditions touched by the deep frost of modernity. Yet it is these survivors, these devotees of a cause and creed assaulted by the Great and the Good, who in the later novels practice an ethic of friendship and cultivate genuine fortitude. They rarely win. Their numbers diminish and their historic territories are lost. But their very resistance, along with the spiritual integrity it attests to, assures the transmission of what is noble, even if those who endure must go underground for centuries. They bury their dead, but not to forget them; they bury their dead with the hope of seeing them rise again.

Reading and defending The Camp of the Saints is not unlike enrolling in one of these little platoons. They are acts of defiance, refusals to submit to the stolid conventions and anemic conformism that dictate the lives of fearful, lesser men. The motive is not mere contrarianism, but the realization that a valuable treasure has been subject to unjust calumnies or condemnations and stands at risk of disappearing forever. We act to stop that disappearance from happening and to save our spiritual heritage. The fruits of these battles are elusive. The penalties for standing firm and fighting on are steep. But to suffer them is a badge of honor.

***

items.title: [Read-along] The Odyssey, W.H.D. Rouse, Books IV - VI
items.text:
*If you've been following along--catch up on the last* [part](https://stacker.news/items/1595925/r/billytheked)*--you probably have found this to be a relaxed pace of reading. Maybe more so than you wish. Alas, life has way of keeping me from this project. As mentioned before, I am reading a hard copy of the translation of W.H.D. Rouse, but I can also recommend the* [*digitized version of the translation of A.S. Kline.*](https://www.poetryintranslation.com/PITBR/Greek/Odhome.php)

***

In the next three books, finally we meet Odysseus, who is (reluctantly?) biding his time on some island with a nymph named Calypso. We hear from his peer, Menelaos and Helen, how Odysseus' heroism and restraint delivered them to victory against the Trojans; however, it becomes harder to distinguish who the true Odysseus really is. His tendency to appear differently from his true nature begins to reveal itself in the stories told about him, and now, first hand, as we are taken along on his adventure to meet the Phaiacians. Thus, we begin to find some truth in the first line of the poem, as translated W.H.D. Rouse, 'here is the story of a man who is never at a loss.' Odysseus begins to earn the name he bears (ὀδύσσομα), whose meaning in Greek translates into something like "to be hated."

## Discussion on Themes

**Hospitality**
The vivid descriptions of feasting, drinking, and making sacrifice to the gods upon the arrival of a guests has defined the escapades of Telemachos up to book IV in the poem. Even as he goes to the house of Menelaos, his good manners and refined appearance precede him, even before he has the chance to make himself known as the son of Odysseus. The Odyssey, being the "national" epic of the Achaeans, takes painstaking effort to provide encyclopedic, lurid descriptions of the level of civilization that had been achieved by Greeks at that time. Clearly, the poem paints a complete and detailed picture of their cultural achievement in the deeply entrenched and refined mores that consistently define what it meant to be Greek. This cultural consistency stands in contrast to the geographic and political separation of the different kingdoms that existed at the time.

**Appearances versus reality**
Finally, in Book V, the reader gets their introduction to Odysseus, who, despite his loyalty to his wife, is on some island playing house with the Nymph Calypso. Since Odysseus rarely presents himself as he truly is, it is impossible for the reader to differentiate whether his desire to return home is authentic, or some hollowed-out sense of moral duty. The reader first learns of his duplicity when Helen recounts how he sneaked into Troy disguised as a beggar, revealing to her their plans to sack the Trojans and rescue her. Also, when Calypso, tells Odysseus he can return home as long as he concedes that his wife is not prettier than her, he lays with her, and doesn't resist. Again, as Odysseus approaches Nausicaa in book VI, he appears as a homeless beggar, in want of proper clothes, when in fact, as we know, Odysseus is the center of attention on Mt Olympus.

**The sea/landscape both as friend and enemy**
There is this sense in the poem that the god of the sea, Earthshaker Poseidon, is the single chaotic force that the Achaeans owe their greatness to, as well as their woes. Nausicaa says to her maids that there is no mortal enemy who do harm on Phaiacia since their country is out of reach, "far away at sea." Also, despite Zeus and Athena's desire to see Odysseus return home, it is grumpy old Poseidon who hurls continued misfortune upon him, as seen after he leaves Calypso. The poem uses the "wine-darkened" sea as a representation of a kind of frontier of civilization, acting at the same time as a buffer of defense, but also a liminal and chaotic realm, where just about anything can happen.

## Questions for contemplation

* **How do you define the frontier of civilization now? Is it a physical place/thing, technological, or something else?**
* **What American national epics document the height of its culture and civilization? How would you characterize these works?**
* **In your opinion, how should we read Odysseus' trickery, as a mark of virtue or a vice?**

# Summaries

## Book IV

Menelaos recounts the death of his brother, Agememnon and laments Odysseus' apparent death, not knowing that he is talking to the latter's very own son. Helen of Troy sedates everyone present with some kind of drug she picked up in Egypt, and tells them the story Odysseus in Troy, where Helen, being held captive, recognized Odysseus disguised as a beggar, who was able to tell her of the Greek's plan to sack the city. Menelaos recounts how he heard her as she circled and touched the Trojan horse, calling our his name, and that if it weren't for Odysseus's being there, urging restraint, he would have called back, blowing their cover. He then tells the story of how he tricked the Old Man of the Sea in Egypt, disguising himself and two of his men with seal carcasses so they can ambush him while he is asleep. The Old Man tells Menelaos of Agememnon's murder, and how Odysseus was still living. Penelope, back in Ithica, prays to Athena, as her suitors plot against Telemachos, laying in wait for his ships to return. Athena summons the ghost of Iphthime, daughter of Icarus, to visit Athena in her sleep to inform her that she will protect Telemachos from harm.

## Book V

Zeus and Athena discuss Odysseus' fate. Zeus reluctantly agrees to intervene to by sending Hermes to inform Calypso of their desire to see Odysseus find his way home, on the condition that Odysseus travel without man or god, and only after a good dose of bad fortune. Calpyso tells Hermes that she loves Odysseus, but does not wish to anger Zeus. She tells Odysseus that it is the god's will that he be allowed to go home, but that he must admit she is prettier than his wife, which he does, and the sleeps with her. Calypso send him off, helping him to hew trees and craft a ship, supplies him with food and wine and water. Poseidon sees Odysseus thus returning, close to his destiny, and decides on shaking up his world, sending a storm his way, to throw him off course. Ino, or Leucothea, the White Sea Goddess, takes pity on him, orders him to strip his clothes and gives him a veil that helps him swim to safety. At first Odysseus refuses, choosing to test his fate and his trusted raft, but this quickly shatters like straw on the threshing floor, and he takes Ino's advice. After he swims to safety, he kisses the earth, returns the veil to Ino, prays to Zeus, and finds a place to take shelter, collapsing from exhaustion.

## Book VI

In the house of Alcinoos, king of the Phaiacians, sleeps his daughter, Nausicaa. Athena visits her in a dream to inspire her to take all of her best bridal linens down to the river to be washed, for the time is coming when she must be prepared to be wed. Thus, Nausicaa appeals to her father, who allows this, prepares for her carts and donkeys. She and her maids take the linens down to a rushing stream, bathe, lather in olive oil, and adorn themselves as the goddess Artemis, daughter of Zeus. They begin playing ball, when Athena decides that it is time that Odysseus is awaken. She causes one of them to drop the ball, sending it hurling down toward the eddies, awakening him. He emerges, craggy and briny, approaches the women, all who get scared away except for Nausicaa, whose fear Athena removed. Odysseus, impressed by her refinement, makes an appeal to her for clothes, which she agrees to. He washes and changes, and Athena makes him taller and more handsome. Finally, the latter invites Odysseus to return to Phaiacia among her party, instructing him to hide in her father's orchard until she makes it back to her father's house. She gives him instructions on how to find her, and tells him he must supplicate himself to her mother if he wishes to return to his own people.

items.title: Plenty of success with square bitcoin payments.
items.text:
Hey guys. Wanted share a nice place on Solomon’s island Maryland called Juice buzz if you’re ever in the area. Here’s their BTCmap: https://btcmap.org/merchant/node:13576086075

I spend bitcoin there often and I am still running into new staff members at the register there. They have the toggle option that makes everything so easy and smooth. I just had a nice interaction and wanted to share.

They make their own great juices so I got one of those and they do smoothies as well. I got a berry blast with creatine. When the lady rung me up she said scan or tap and I responded with the same thing I always do here:

Actually I’m gunna pay with bitcoin, isn’t that cool?

That is cool! She exclaimed, which made me smile.

So she presented the pay page, I toggled to Bitcoin, and having pre-opened my Phoenix wallet I scanned it right away. I like to hold the phone up so they can see me press pay and witness the speed.

She gasped and said Wow that was really fast!

Right?!

Then I like to give a cool spiel that always seems to be accepted well without me feeling or acting like a salesman.

I told her that jack Dorsey is the creator of cash app and also square and he is a nice advocate for bitcoin—new information for her.

I told her what’s cool here is that we are using an inclusive network. Before, in order to interact with a Cash App bar code, I would need cash app. Venmo to Venmo. Cash app to Cash App. Examples of exclusive networks. But what’s cool about Bitcoin is anyone can use it and in many different ways. You can use any one of the hundreds of apps out there like I did or if you have the skill and desire you can build your own and interact in the same way we just did.

She was interested! But she did say skeptically: yeah I’m not really too sure about bitcoin.

I said that’s understandable. It’s weird and intimidating and controversial and there’s lots to learn.

I continued to say one of my favorite things about Bitcoin though is that anyone can use it. Your age, sex, race, religion, location matters not. Bitcoin will work for anyone without permission or ID.

She asked: but do you need cash app to have Bitcoin?

No, Bitcoin is completely separate from everything else I said. And left it at that.

Juice buzz is owned by Dana the owner of the Blue Wind Gormet. I wrote about her and that place twice in the past. Here’s the links:

https://stacker.news/items/1436254/r/SatAttack

https://stacker.news/items/1472530

These places right now are my favorite places to spend sats. As far as I know Dana is still keeping the bitcoin she receives through her square terminals and isn’t converting. I have tried to encourage her to buy honey from [https://sweetsats.io](https://sweetsats.io), a bee farm in Maine, to use in both of her stores so she can have somewhere to spend her sats, but I don’t think it’s happened yet.

items.title: Austin trip day six: lakes, hikes, final bitcoin meal.
items.text:
Hey stackers,

I write from the airport terminal in route to the chilly easy coast. What an incredible trip this has been. I’m normally looking forward to getting back home and returning to the recurrence of every day life. Not this time. I am not ready to leave and I know I’ll be back. Perhaps to live one day.

Yesterday morning I woke up at 3 AM a little hung over from all my wine at III forks and I couldn’t sleep. So I went to play poker. Got there at 4 AM and the crowd was wild. Everyone had been there since the night before and everyone seemed drunk, tired, or both. I played this huge hand and ended up winning a $1400 pot. https://stacker.news/items/1606387/r/SatAttack?commentId=1606424

I played until about 7 AM and headed out for breakfast. I ended up at a really nice diner called Phoebes diner and had a great meal. Forgot take pictures though. They sell slab bacon and serve it in thick deep fried slices. Wonderful. I get back to the hotel and sleep from 830AM to 12PM. @grayruby had recommended I take the 30 minute drive to visit lake Travis. After poking around on my phone for things around there I found a hike and a restaurant I wanted to do.

Here’s the all trail for the hike: [river place nature trail](https://www.alltrails.com/trail/us/texas/river-place-canyon-trail?sh=true)

The hike ended up being a great success. The weather was great and it was just the right amount of challenging to get the heart pumping.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164323)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164324)

I’ll take a little time to plug the Earth Runners here. For all my barefoot maxis out there this is a wonderful footwear for rocky environments where bare feet may have a tough time. I have taken these everywhere in all sorts of terrain. Love them.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164326)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164327)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164328)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164329)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164330)

Awesome hike. I was pleased to find good water flow and was surprised how clear it was! That tree going across the path is called the noggin knocker and there was a sign warning you not to knock your noggin haha.

Finishing my hike I was very ready for food and water and headed out to a restaurant right on Lake Travis called The Oasis. I didn’t really know what I was getting myself into but this place was GRAND. It’s a massive four story restaurant that’s the size of a big hotel. All four stories have a balcony that over looks the lake. There’s awesome art and decorations everywhere.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164331)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164332)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164333)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164334)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164335)

On my way in there was this blue metal UFO thing covered in stickers. I took the opportunity to put one of the stickers @k00b gave me on there. Turned out nice I think.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164336)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164337)

The food was decent. I got the chips and salsa. (Great chips!!) the chicken enchiladas with rice and beans, and a margarita on the rocks. I wasn’t planning on drinking but… the view made me.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164338)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164339)

I got back to my hotel around 6 pm and slept until 830. I had been deliberating between going to play poker one last time or going to find one last place to spend some sats. The issue was they were in opposite directions and I was really torn for a while. With one last check of BTCmaps I found a great solution. A place called Rockin Rolls that wasn’t in the downtown areas! It was close enough to the hotel and poker room to do both. So off I went. Here’s the BTCmap link [https://btcmap.org/merchant/node:13309320506](https://btcmap.org/merchant/node:13309320506)
It’s a small food truck in small gathering of food trucks right off the road. I appreciated the abundance of parking here!

![](https://m.stacker.news/164342)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164343)

These guys are awesome and if you’re a pizza eater in Austin I recommend giving this one a try. They make sourdough pizza rolls and they are very good. I ordered three classics (pepperoni and cheese) and a mini cannoli. Now time to pay. I see they only have the small white square terminal and I won’t be presented with the toggle option so I tell the man I’d like to pay with bitcoin if I can… he isn’t sure and calls the owner over who was thankfully there. He says “I think I set that up …” and we collectively poke around the terminal. Doesn’t take us long to find Bitcoin listed as one of the payment options and I tell them all we have to do is click that and it should generate me a QR code. It did and I made another seemless Phoenix payment. I gave my small spiel about how cool this is and how anyone who knows how can interact with this terminal with a bunch of different options.

The owner, Jake, was impressed and pleased. He was excited to see bitcoin being used and told me I was the first to do it. But on BTCmaps someone had verified the location in November 2025 so I was thinking perhaps not. I showed him BTCmaps and his little page on there and he thought that was very cool too! I told him that I would be blogging about this day and experience on stacker news and gave him the lowdown about what goes on here. “That sounds right my ally” he said. He loves community and according to him he likes crypto. He’s an ethereum guy he says. I told him I don’t know anything about it because I haven’t been able to move past Bitcoin. I was explaining what SN was and he understood immediately. “So instead of a like you just send over a little satoshi?” YEAH! I gave him a SN sticker and told him how to find us and that if he ever had any questions or inquires about using bitcoin in his business or other wise this is the place to come. I told him he would be very welcomed as a business owner accepting sats.

When I got my order I realized I didn’t have a drink. I asked for a bottle of water and had opened my Phoenix wallet to pay but he just said don’t worry about it. Thanks Jake!

I’ll say again, if you like pizza, come try this place. It’s awesome and he was telling me he’s looking to move to another state. Him and his wife love Austin but they’ve been there for 20 years and are ready for change. So time is running out!

![](https://m.stacker.news/164347)

After my pizza rolls it was time for one last poker sesh. I headed back to the lodge card club and played an uneventful 1.5 hours and won $10. I got gas for  the Turo rental, got to my hotel around 1130, and packed up. I had to be up at 530 to head to the airport.

I enjoyed my time in Austin very much and I really enjoyed sharing my experience here on stackers!! I’ve gotten a lot of support and a lot of engagement and that has been sweet. Thanks for reading and thank you to those who gave me awesome suggestions. I tried to do them all.

If you missed the other trip reports here they are:

Day one:
https://stacker.news/items/1602995/r/SatAttack

Day two: https://stacker.news/items/1603699/r/SatAttack

Day three: https://stacker.news/items/1604324/r/SatAttack

Day four and five: https://stacker.news/items/1605873/r/SatAttack

items.title: Tether Fun Unbelievable Details - Part VI
items.text:
*This is part of a larger series on the history of Tether. Part I (*https://stacker.news/items/1042943*), Part II (*https://stacker.news/items/1059310*), Part III (*https://stacker.news/items/1115791*), Part IV (*https://stacker.news/items/1410689/*), Part V (*https://stacker.news/items/1613156*)*

# 19 CANTOR FITZGERALD

19.1   On 1 December 2021, Rumble Inc., [announces](https://www.cantor.com/rumble-inc-the-neutral-video-platform-to-go-public-through-combination-with-cantor-fitzgeralds-cf-acquisition-corp-vi-nasdaq-cfvi/) it will go public through combination with Cantor Fitzgerald's CF Acquisition Corp. VI.

19.11   "Rumble is designed to be the rails and independent infrastructure that is immune to cancel culture. We are a movement that does not stifle, censor, or punish creativity and believe everyone benefits from access to a neutral network with diverse ideas and opinions. We are on a mission to restore the internet to its roots by making it free and open once again. The transaction we announced today will provide Rumble with the additional capital necessary to continue to scale our business and carry out our mission." [--Chris Pavlovski, Founder and CEO of Rumble](https://www.cantor.com/rumble-inc-the-neutral-video-platform-to-go-public-through-combination-with-cantor-fitzgeralds-cf-acquisition-corp-vi-nasdaq-cfvi/)

19.111   "The CF VI Board has unanimously approved and adopted the Business Combination Agreement and unanimously recommends that our stockholders vote “FOR” each of the Proposals presented to CF VI Stockholders." [-Amendment No. 1 to Form 2-4 Registration Statement under the Securities Act of 1933 for CF Acquisition Corp. VI](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1830081/000121390022026101/fs42022a1_cfacquisition6.htm)

19.12   Howard Lutnick [says](https://www.cantor.com/rumble-inc-the-neutral-video-platform-to-go-public-through-combination-with-cantor-fitzgeralds-cf-acquisition-corp-vi-nasdaq-cfvi/) "Rumble is the most exciting social media and video distribution platform in the market today."

19.13   "Today Rumble enters a new era. We partnered with Tether, a company that exports American values to the entire world, and who are major advocates for free speech." [--Chris Pavlovski](https://x.com/chrispavlovski/status/1870249250241511654)

19.131   Rumble [announces](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1830081/000121390024111298/ea022562201ex99-1_rumble.htm) $775 million strategic investment from Tether.

19.132   "Most people don't realize Tether is a Bitcoin company that happens to do other things like Ai, energy, and stablecoins." [--Samson Mow](https://x.com/Excellion/status/1870577229367005648)

19.133   "Beyond our initial shareholder stake, Tether intends to drive towards a meaningful advertising, cloud, and crypto payment solutions relationship with Rumble." [--Paolo Ardoino](https://www.rum.group/blog/rumble-announces-775-million-strategic-investment-from-tether/)

19.134   "Tether deeply believes in the fundamental values of freedom of speech and financial freedom." [--Paolo Ardoino](https://x.com/paoloardoino/status/1870231681497538759)

19.135   Rumble [closes](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1830081/000121390025011371/ea023027801ex99-1_rumble.htm) the $775 million strategic investment from Tether on 7 February 2025.

19.14   Tether's 2023 Q4 attestation [reports](https://tether.io/news/tethers-2023-q4-attestation/) $2.85 billion in profit.

19.2   "There's a company that I like called Tether." [-Howard Lutnick](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/videos/2024-01-16/lutnick-the-fed-is-staying-higher-for-longer-video)

19.21   "I manage many, many of their assets. And Tether Holdings is the name of the group, And the group, from what we've seen, and we did a lot of work, they have the money they say they have. In the last attestation they said they had $86 billion of assets and $83 billion of liabilities, and I've seen and the firm has seen a whole lot and they have the money. So there's always been a lot of talk saying 'Do they have it or not?' so I'm with you guys saying, 'We've seen it. And they have it.'" [-Howard Lutnick](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/videos/2024-01-16/lutnick-the-fed-is-staying-higher-for-longer-video)

19.211   "I basically told him the movie line. I said, ‘Show me the money,’" Lutnick told a crypto conference in July. "And we found every penny, and they had every penny, but they had it in what I would call pretty godforsaken places," he said, noting Tether’s holdings of short-term loans to Chinese companies, known as commercial paper. [-Howard Lutnick in *The Wall Street Journal*](https://archive.is/rSRx1#selection-5681.0-5681.330)

19.2111   On 10 February 2023, The Wall Street Journal [reports](https://archive.is/4wyww) that Cantor Fitzgerald helps oversee Tether's $39 billion in Treasury holdings.

19.212   The Wall Street Journal also [reports](https://archive.is/4wyww) that Tether "began moving its reserves into the Wall Street brokerage in late 2021, around the time it reached a settlement with a regulator, one of the people said."

19.2121   And [that](https://archive.is/4wyww) Cantor is one of the 25 so-called primary dealers for the U.S. Treasurys market, a status that allows them to trade directly with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and underwrite sales of U.S. government debt.

19.213   "Tether and Cantor had established a relationship in 2021 when Cantor began acting as a custodian and trading partner for a portion of the U.S. treasuries backing Tether’s stablecoin reserves. In late November and early December 2024, representatives of Cantor and Tether, also representing Bitfinex, had ordinary course meetings to discuss various topics, including their existing relationship, where they also engaged in discussions regarding the formation and operation of a public company that would include holding and acquiring Bitcoin as part of its business operations, including the contribution by each of Tether and Bitfinex of 10,000 Bitcoin to such a business. Cantor advised Tether that it would explore the various ways to bring such a company public and present a proposed structure to Tether." [-Proxy Statement for Extraordinary General Meeting of Shareholders of Cantor Equity Partners, Inc. and Prospectus for up to 315,116,673 shares of Class A common stock of Twenty One Capital, Inc.](https://www.cstproxy.com/cantorequitypartners/2025/proxy/images/Cantor_Equity_Partners_Inc-EGMProxy2025.pdf)

19.214   In 2021, Tether "secured an account with Cantor Fitzgerald, and started converting its commercial paper assets to U.S. Treasury bills. Cantor had existing ties to Tether through its sister firm, BGC Partners, a trading desk that had bought and sold large volumes of Tether, according to a source with knowledge of the relationship." [-Forbes](https://archive.is/KU9ap)

19.2141   "Tether and Cantor had established a relationship in 2021 when Cantor began acting as a custodian and trading partner for a portion of the U.S. treasuries backing." [-Twenty One Capital, Inc. Draft Registration Statement on Form S-4](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2070457/000000000025008030/filename1.pdf)

19.2142   "Tether has additionally been using New York financial services giant Cantor Fitzgerald as a custodian of U.S. Treasury bills, three sources said." [--Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/davidjeans/2023/02/10/tether-reserves-cantor-capital-union-ansbacher/)

19.2143   "Cantor Fitzgerald has been a Tether custodian since late 2021, Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino told The Block." [--The Block](https://www.theblock.co/news/markets/2024-01-16-cantor-fitzgerald-ceo-tether-reserves-272893)

19.2144   "Cantor custodies "the vast vast majority" of Tether's reserves, a person with direct knowledge of the matter told The Block." [--The Block](https://www.theblock.co/news/markets/2024-01-16-cantor-fitzgerald-ceo-tether-reserves-272893)

19.22   "Devasini has credited \[Richard] Heathcote with playing a key part in establishing the relationship with Cantor, a person with knowledge of the matter said. Heathcote acknowledged helping to connect the two firms while at Marlin Capital, adding that Lutnick was personally involved in the grueling due diligence process. Cantor started managing Tether’s reserves in 2021, media reports have said." [-Bloomberg](https://businessmirror.com.ph/2025/05/13/tethers-150b-cio-proved-himself-getting-cantor-backing/)

19.221   "Heathcote helped build Tether’s giant T-bill operation into an entity almost on autopilot: Buy bills with on average below 90 days duration at auction, hold until maturity, then repeat. 'It’s really not rocket science,' he said." [-Bloomberg](https://businessmirror.com.ph/2025/05/13/tethers-150b-cio-proved-himself-getting-cantor-backing/)

19.222   "Heathcote also played a key role nurturing Tether’s increasingly close relationship with Cantor Fitzgerald LP." [-Bloomberg](https://businessmirror.com.ph/2025/05/13/tethers-150b-cio-proved-himself-getting-cantor-backing/)

19.223   "HEATHCOTE, a graduate of Newcastle University, joined Tether as CIO in January 2023, succeeding Silvano di Stefano. He first met Tether Chief Executive Officer Paolo Ardoino and Chairman Giancarlo Devasini around 2018 while working as head of trading at Bahamas-based Deltec Bank & Trust, one of Tether’s banks." [-Bloomberg](https://businessmirror.com.ph/2025/05/13/tethers-150b-cio-proved-himself-getting-cantor-backing/)

19.224   "He left Deltec in 2019 and later set up fund-management and advisory firm Marlin Capital Partners, bringing Tether as a client with him." [-Bloomberg](https://businessmirror.com.ph/2025/05/13/tethers-150b-cio-proved-himself-getting-cantor-backing/)

19.2241   "Previously, he was the Chief Executive Officer at BankPro Limited, where he was responsible for the overall management and launch of the digital banking and investment products. Prior to BankPro, Richard was the Head of Trading at Deltec Bank and Trust. Whilst there he rebuilt the bank’s multi-asset trading business culminating in over $20bn of flow in 2019. He also co-led the building of the bank’s capitalized Institutional Asset Management business with desk peak assets of $4bn. items.title: There is No Such Thing as Price Gouging: Airline Shutdown Edition
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/166604)

![](https://m.stacker.news/166605)

I saw a lot of economically ignorant tweets surrounding the recent shutdown of all flights nationwide by the FAA, so it's good time to re-iterate: there is no such thing as price gouging.

The rise in price of Ubers, hotel rooms, or supplies during any kind emergency is simply the product of demand rapidly rising, while supply remains fixed in the short term. Anyone who has seen a supply & demand graph can understand this phenomenon.

![](https://m.stacker.news/166611)

Moreover, it is good for victims of a disaster if you allow prices to rise.

Let's say a hurricane hits town, and the price of a gallon jug of water goes from $1 to $10. People from other towns will see an opportunity, and bring supplies from their town to sell for profit. But if you ban it under the guise of "price gouging," you're killing the incentive to do so, and, ironically, depriving the affected people of needed supplies. You're also creating a perverse incentive for whomever gets the store first to buy up a larger supply of water than they personally need, just because it's so cheap.

items.title: Bitcoin Arena: decentralized game & prediction market platform live on testnet4
items.text:
Hi there,

We built Bitcoin Arena: games and prediction markets on Bitcoin. It is fully decentralized. There is no company running the rounds, no central server and no custodian. Anyone can run a node, and anyone can offer an app. It’s live on testnet4, and we need people outside the team to try both.

There’s no token and nothing to buy. Test sats are free and have no value.

Anyone can run a node

* Install it on Windows, macOS or Linux. A setup window walks you through it.
* Post a bond on Bitcoin and take a seat.
* Host apps, verify rounds and earn a share of the fees.
* No permission needed. Your bond is your ticket in.

Anyone can offer an app

* Write your game and sign it, and any node can host it.
* The nodes replay every round with your rules.
* There’s no approval and no listing fee.
* You earn 2% of every paid round in your app.

How a round stays honest

* A Bitcoin block hash draws the committee of nodes, so nobody picks who decides.
* Stakes lock in a Fedimint federation run by the nodes.
* A result counts only when 5 of 7 nodes confirm the same one, and anyone can object for 10 minutes.

How you can help

* Run a node on testnet4 and tell us where setup was hard.
* Build a small app and tell us what’s missing in the docs.
* Play Tick Tock Next Block, Rock Paper Scissors or the 15-minute Bitcoin Up or Down market and try to break it.

Would you run a node or build an app on this? If not, what’s stopping you? Honest criticism helps us most. Reply here or join us:
