items.title: [REVIEW] V for Vendetta by Alan Moore and David Lloyd
items.text:
**Normally, I try to avoid spoilers in my reviews. This one has spoilers.**

![](https://m.stacker.news/164947)

V is cool and all and his vendetta against Big Brother is a great story, but there's one part of this that I just can't get out of my mind. In the middle of the story, Evey is captured and thrown in a prison where she is interrogated, tortured, presented with a false confession, and told to sign. She refuses. She doesn't betray V. And so she is told that she is going to be taken out back and shot.

It's a horrible moment. Till now, V has always swooped in to save the day. And throughout Evey's horrible captivity and torture, we keep expecting V to show up and put a stop to it, with knives, mayhem and murder. But, this time, he doesn't show.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164948)

So it seems like this is the end. Evey chooses to stand for what she believes in, even though it means she will die. But then:

![](https://m.stacker.news/164949)

This is a weird twist. But it quickly turns dark when Evey walks through her prison door...and into V's sitting room:

![](https://m.stacker.news/164950)

We knew V was not the most even-keeled individual, but this is messed up. What the hell is going on?

> "Happiness is a prison, Evey. Happiness is the most insidious prison of all."

V has this moment where he completely flips Evey's worldview:

> "I didn't put you in a prison, Evey. I just showed you the bars...You were born in a prison. You've been in a prison so long, you no longer believe there's a world outside...You can feel freedom closing in upon you. You're afriad because freedom is terrifying."

I really struggled with this scene. Evey's conversion seems so unbelievable to me. Why should she see this new injustice (V's little false-flag operation on her) as anything other than the same sort of brutal, banal, boring violence brought down upon her by someone else? Is it that this time she accepted death, no longer trying to bargain with the system? Or that in this case it came upon her from someone she trusted, a quarter she thought was safe?

At first, I thought this was a sort of ends-justify-the-means argument: V's still the good guy here because putting her in a cell and waterboarding her and telling her she's going to be shot gets her to the point where she can be truly free. And it is sort of that, but not entirely.

There's also the blunt force thought that hardship, extreme hardship is a necessary step to freedom -- even perhaps that you can't have freedom without it. This is terrifying because it makes me worry that I am one of the prisoners who would rather remain a prisoner. Because life in prison is happy enough. Maybe you can't get to the freedom without the hardship.

Evey's conversion is successful because the stakes were so high -- she couldn't come to value her life until it was actually on the line. 

This is pretty directly relevant to Bitcoin -- especially this year: if Bitcoin is our shot at freedom, why do we think it will come easy and without terror? Using Bitcoin means you using something designed to break the law. Holding your own keys means you can lose your own keys. 

It's a nice story...but is it true?

items.title: When Saying "Yes" Cost Me $3: On Business Ethics & the Economics of Optimization
items.text:
**I have some reflections on optimization-economics on SN:**

* [“On the Economics of Peer-to-Peer, pt 2: The Stubborn Issue of Indexation](https://stacker.news/items/1552045)”
* “[On the Economics of Peer-to-Peer: I Tried Vexl](https://stacker.news/items/1405015)”

…and another, recently, about Invity https://stacker.news/items/1604577 — the Czech-based fintech/bitcoin-savings vehicle that’s making some serious noise this side of the pond — and *doing what’s good for a customer.* (To recap that one, they have sleek marketing and a nice array of products and offerings to help Bitcoiners stack, and good, transparent fees... *except* the hidden spread, which is outrageously large.)

Look, I understand that under ruthless dog-eats-dog capitalism, businesses are under no obligation (morally or legally) to be *good* to a customer… other than, you know, it being in their long-term interest of forging lasting relationships and other such nice trust/extra-market things.

**What I don’t understand is why businesses sometimes try to *sneak* their customers and pull a fast one on them.** How is that going to endear me to you? Isn’t it better to do that is good so that I come back for more?

Standard philosophy setting is you sit down at a random normal restaurant and, *without checking the fine print of the menu,* order a beer and a burger... and then have a heart attack **when the bill arrives at $1,000.** Reasonable? Your fault? *You didn't check the menu, silly*! *It clearly states that sit-in customers (on a full moon??) with beer and burger pay standard $1,000)* [https://stacker.news/items/159812\&#x33](https://stacker.news/items/159812&#x33);*,* https://stacker.news/items/1586158

To quote Sam Rogers (Kevin Spacey) in *Margin Call*: “You will never sell to any of those people ever again” *and later*: [*“you damn well know that you don't make a sale unless you think the guy is gonna come back for more, and tomorrow we are done.”*](https://imsdb.com/scripts/Margin-Call.html#:~:text=you%20damn%20well%20know%20that%20you%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20don%27t%20make%20a%20sale%20unless%20you%20think%20the%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20guy%20is%20gonna%20come%20back%20for%20more%2C%20and%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20tomorrow%20we%20are%20done.)

***

An exchange or marketplace, for instance, is in the business of matching buyers and sellers (https://stacker.news/items/1603314). Yes, there are TX fees; yes there are all manner of accessory services they can sell and fees (“connection or setup costs”) they can charge dealers or banks or traders… *and*, importantly (https://stacker.news/items/1604577) **a buy-ask** [**spread**](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/s/spread.asp)**.**

*To briefly bring everyone up to speed:* When you buy an asset on a marketplace or from a dealer, you pay *slightly* above its current market price, say $100.25 if the thing is trading at 100; when you sell it back to that same marketplace or dealer, at a neat little 10% pop profit perhaps, you pocket $109.75. The dealer *lives* on that small difference, since all they do every day is sell and buy to everyone.

Today I was in the closest town. I had some leftover dollars from the summer, and it was finally time to deposit them in a bank that takes (FX) cash. I have done this before and I have a USD account with them. Exchanging them for local currency at my convenience later usually costs me a small, immaterial spread (0.5% if I recall correctly). Today, I also had some local currency in cash, so I thought I’d deposit them in the regular current account at the same time. When the teller asked me, **“Deposited straight into current account?” I didn’t think much further and just responded, “Yes.”**

## Little did I think that *this* meek, silly, foreign-language affirmative would cost me some $3.

Because when I stepped outside and looked at the receipt, the exchange rate the lady had used was *not* the neat little 1.5%-ish pop that the DXY had so gracefully given us this week… but a rate 4.4% *below* market. So had I clarified that I wanted these USD to sit in USD, *at the USD account*, and me exchanging them once I got home, I would have paid a \~4% smaller spread.

Now, this wasn’t **any extra service or special benefit to me**, but a clear cash grab. And the annoying bit is that the bank *already makes money off its regular spread*... Why do you get to take another 4% because I accidentally said "Yes" at the counter and *you* clicked the button instead of me? That's not work, that's not value add.

I don’t understand why this is a thing? And if it’s a pure customer-inattention cash grab/punishment, why isn’t it 10%? 15?

***

I can get *unreasonably* annoyed over things like this… annoyed at myself, annoyed at the world, annoyed at the person/company on the other side of the transaction.... (I *think* I wrote about this on SN somewhere, https://stacker.news/items/1463559, https://stacker.news/items/1598123?commentId=1598194).

*Background*: Revolut, the European fintech wonder (that earlier this year blocked my account for two weeks on unfounded money-laundering slip-ups… https://stacker.news/items/1417296) gives me some amount of made-up points for every purchase — the spending of which I then feel saddled to optimize for.

When turned into discounts in their own Booking.com-like accommodation service, they have some fiat-money value; when transferred to airlines I regularly use, they have a different (and ever-changing) value — usually in the range of 0.5-2% of the initial spend necessary to “generate” the points.

For every Revolut Stays (https://stacker.news/items/1463559) or airport lounge access or RevolutPay Uber ride, Revolut offers to exchange some of their made-up points for discounts.
(Recently, I was offered three levels of 0.6%, 0.8% and 1.2% “returns” on redeeming my discounts. I also have the recurring options of turning them into miles at my regular airlines — SAS https://stacker.news/items/1613346, Icelandair, Finnair — where I’m giving *their* shitcoins to redeem for discounts on airfares. Usually, these are worth around 0.2%-0.6% of the transaction value necessary to obtain them.)

**A few months back, I ordered an Uber and clicked through everything superfast,** since I had to make it to a train station in time. From the corner of my eye, I noticed that there was a “Revolut Pay: 10x” payment option, but I was concerned with catching my train so I ignored it. Turned out, this was another avenue in which Revolut has been trying to get into the (very lucrative!) payment business, and to get their customers to help out, they “bribe” them with 10x the regular amount of make-up points. I lost out on my €25 spend, and could have netted a neat 5%-ish benefit if I had had my wits about me and not been stressed.

## The point is that while the “loss” was minor, it *annoyed me for days*.

At least in *this* story, our incentives are aligned: Revolut *wants me* to pay with their preferred payment option rather than resorting to Mastercard/Visa; my local bank, however, *wants* to grab as much and as juicy fees as possible.

I dunno, man. 

No good solution, no smart econ insight. Just healthy venting and metaphysical little question of *why* we don’t all get along and help each other out? https://stacker.news/items/1559053 https://stacker.news/items/1552045

items.title: I Used to Be a Progress Man. No More (The Daily Economy, Joakim Book)
items.text:
aaaah, the attentive stackers could have seen this coming a while ago (https://stacker.news/items/1599758)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164902)

Basically a public breakup with the tech-optimistic humanprogress types. For *years*, I've struggled trying to write something for HumanProgress.org, one of the outlets I've written for a lot in the past. 

I just **can't,** anymore: it's so naive, so "*raw-raw*, look at this irrelevant techno-crappy improvement over here." \<insert *It's all fine* dog meme.>

VERY excited and grateful that I could lay out the case in print and explain, seriously and particularly, why the constant Tupy-Follett-Omary-Pooley-Morley-Crawford stuff celebrating, well, *anything* as good and improving.

I know the *exact* moment when this flip started shifting in reverse for me. (Ask me about it IRL some time.) It's been brewing for a few years.

***

> I have written something like 25 articles for [HumanProgress.org](http://humanprogress.org/), the first of which had the title “[Worldviews Are Pessimistic Because They Are Outdated.](https://humanprogress.org/a-much-needed-update-to-our-outdated-worldviews/)” I used to breathe Matt Ridley’s [*The Rational Optimist*](https://www.amazon.com/Rational-Optimist-How-Prosperity-Evolves/dp/1665102632)*,* and I’ve forced more than one unwilling family member to take [Hans Rosling](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/i-wish-that-hans-rosling-were-still-alive/)’s [Gapminder test](https://www.gapminder.org/tag/gapminder-test/) on global development.
>
> These days, I find that article’s subheading the most important bit: “When making sense of the world, we operate *on decades-old information.*” I’m gradually coming around to the view that I didn’t do my homework the first time around, and that *that* article was based “on decades-old information.”

Most of the metrics human progress-types rely on have stalled for decades. The *improvements* and amazing achievements of humanity are OLD NEWS -- they happened a long time ago. And actually, looking at the things that matter (objectively; not value judgment), it's not at all obvious that humans (in the West...) are improving much.

Actually, we might be *regressing* quite a bit. https://stacker.news/items/1601880. And we're running out of time turning that shit around https://stacker.news/items/1579572

![](https://m.stacker.news/164903)

Most obviously, the price indices people use to confidently establish how much better we are, are clearly broken. Bitcoiners know that. Economists know that. I think *even the humanprogress-type people* know that. https://stacker.news/items/1566496. But yet, they insist on trying to carve out fantastical measures in which, like, the cost of a Thanksgiving dinner non-quality-adjusted labor hours, for the increasingly fewer people working.

And if you follow the logic and evidence -- being dispassionate analysts, https://stacker.news/items/1607775, https://stacker.news/items/1606098 etc -- we're not (that much?) better off. And in quite a lot of respects, *worse* off. In the article, I point to several metrics humanprogress types always chant as amazing progress: **child mortality and working hours**. Both are correct, just outdated: child mortality hasn't improved in a generation, working hours in the most successful, wealthy/rich countries are flat for twenty years 
(They're only falling in economic basket cases like Germany, Britain, and South Korea, where government policies and green delusions have *pushed* them down... by making value-added work not worth it anymore. https://stacker.news/items/1593954)

**"The improvements of modernity are real; the timing just isn’t."**

## "in most countries there has been *no progress* in working hours over the last twenty-odd years; all the improvements come from the 1960s, ’70s, and ’80s."

> Most of the grim old days that Follett writes about in her book with that title are *from centuries ago*. Yes, compared to my ancestors who eked out a subsistence life from farming the harsh, unforgiving, and disastrously poor Nordic nature, I am miles better off. But so were my parents’ generation; and it’s not obvious that *compared to them*, my [peers and I are doing much better](https://capx.co/complaints-about-the-generational-divide-obscure-a-much-more-positive-picture). **With the obvious exception of communication tech and screens, we have the same appliances, yet can afford fewer or, at best, the same amount of stuff they could.**

Knock me down with a feather. 

***

But my real beef with these guys is that they IGNORE the obviously deteriorating and really-bad-stuff happening right before our eyes. And no, I'm not talking about climate change (I'm not retarded... https://stacker.news/items/1603339):

> In political governance and my own domains of monetary and fiscal matters, we have *definitely* regressed: the out-of-control fiscal deficits in every major country, bond yields exploding, and the [very awkward](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/the-fed-may-pause-but-inflation-wont/), [botched, post-pandemic](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/fed-admits-it-was-wrong-kind-of/) double-digit inflation are just the most obvious misdoings. Depending only a little on your ideological stance, the [ratchet effect](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/covid-19s-ratchet-effect-is-becoming-endemic/) and relentless expansion in [government spending as a share of GDP](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/historical-gov-spending-gdp?tab=line&time=1900..latest&country=JPN~USA~DEU~GBR~ISL~FIN~FRA) are a poor stand-in for “progress.” Britain, ever the role model for decline, is [hitting tax extraction levels](https://stacker.news/items/1602493) (north of 35 percent) not seen since fighting a literal world war.

> No matter what AI-fueled productivity growth may be forecast going forward, America *cannot* outgrow its $40 trillion [government debt](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/america-cant-outgrow-40-trillion-in-debt/), as Pete Earle demonstrated in a [fiscal arithmetic piece](https://civl.com/partners/growing-out-of-40-trillion-some-unpleasant-fiscal-arithmetic-4564ea48) for CiVL — to say nothing of the stagnating, struggling, and literally burning European countries stuck in a [bond yield-fiscal deficit spiral](https://ft.com/content/9b252b46-a87c-45e7-a09a-45a39ce077b8).

***

TL;DR:

> **Almost all the improvements in human welfare in the last thirty years happened in digital gadgets and communication** — and the jury is still out on whether Netflix to the masses and social media to teenagers (let alone adults) were, [on net](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/return-to-reality-the-economy-is-pivoting-amid-digital-overload/), good or bad. We’re paying for it dearly in [mental health epidemics](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/mental-health-is-in-crisis-what-is-the-answer/), broken societies, and a viciously divided polity. *Where, I repeat, is this human progress?*

The ultimate test has always been: *Would you trade places with someone in the past? What's the best time to be alive?* And the answer, to me -- having always answered, Barack Obama style, **no** + **today/tomorrow** --
is increasingly... *yes*. 

Victorian England (https://stacker.news/items/1591235) or fin-de-siècle Vienna have always been dreamy epochs for me, the lack of modern appliances and warmth and health etc aside; the post-war boomer exuberance and sense of progress is appealing; but even the very simple "20 years ago" passes the test  **It's not at all obvious to me that we're better off/live better lives today than in 2006.**

items.title: Are You Having Fun Staying Poor, Stackers?
items.text:
*Alternative title: **how do you tell the difference between a blip/dip and a final and complete collapse?***

This is *not* (primarily) a reflection on bitcoin's price debacle or the unwinding of the AI bubble or anything else going on in financial markets. The themes are, of course, overlapping and not unrelated/coincidental... but what *I'm getting at is life choices and professional "investments"/bets* and how to consider your situation etc (https://stacker.news/items/1617542).

...let’s start with our friend Jason Hodlers (@geekigai) and his call for help yesterday. It both disturbs me and generates a ton of empathy… “awfully relatable,” I wrote to a friend as I shared it, but also feeling really iffy it... (words like "reckless", "justice", "unfair", and "audacious" coming to mind.)

https://x.com/geekigai/status/2123313407927435724

Not in that *I am* in his situation, or have a dislocated shoulder, or have a family to support but that **you sacrifice the professional path you were on to do something you deeply believed in**. That’s admirable: we all want it, we certainly all want it to *work out,* and we celebrate those who do.... and those of us who do it (https://stacker.news/items/1513929) in *this* industry tell you over and over that you shouldn’t, it’s not all it’s made out to be, and actually *doing literally anything else* might be both financially better and professionally more secure.

Still, here we are and for some of us it goes *terribly* wrong.

You always gotta make a choice and a gamble: what industry to go for, what to study/learn, what career path, and in what country? **What are you good at, and what can you offer the world?**

## But what happens if what you have to offer isn't valued by others, or suddenly outcompeted by some technical advancement you didn't (couldn't) foresee?

AI has been hot and flourishing for years, and you were probably a geeky loser if you were into LLMs in the 2010s; bitcoin has been briefly hot now and again, but most of the time you're just a loser, having wasted your life and life savings on some stupid little internet experiment.

Jason describes how he and his wife — who is homeschooling some number of kids (because “god told us to” -- LOL. @. Dat) and has no ties to the labor market — two years ago decided that he should step down from his (fiat?) work and “focus all my time on building a local Bitcoin circular economy through @bitcoinchatt”.

Sure, we know how these things pan out — they don’t! — so that might have been reckless. But if/when this thing actually was a once-in-a-species monetary revolution, then this sort of local support/educational group would have been invaluable, picks-and-shovels style. And kudos to him for trying to build something real (and not financialized... not looking at anything or anyone in particular https://stacker.news/items/1617030)

…and when money got tight, he cleaned Airbnbs. Then fell and injured himself, so then he did even crappier jobs (on commission) that didn’t pay much… and then the thing he had built more or less fell apart.

Not able to buy groceries, he is “turning to the Bitcoin plebs for help”

> I have so little money right now (100% in bitcoin, except for some pocket change), I've hardly even felt this dip.

***

As @benmuse has been showing us — and the twitterati cope cheerleaders won’t shut up about — calm DCA **over long periods** has been pretty great in bitcoin (https://stacker.news/items/1616043). Problem: most of that benefit (not unlike the progress convo I’m having off-Bitcoin (https://stacker.news/items/1608876, https://stacker.news/items/1616353 ) came *years ago*. “Getting into bitcoin” this year or last has proved disastrous.

https://x.com/Bitcoin_phan/status/2123546470976766236

Yes, during the 2022 low-point we could *at least* blame the crazy frauds and paper bitcoin (https://stacker.news/items/1617378) and rates getting off zero, but in 2024-26 *everything* was set for this thing to work. If, at any point in bitcoin’s history, you wanted to sketch out the conditions under which we win, it would have *these* elements (ETFs, recognition, political turning point, regulatory clarity, *all these incredible services* etc etc) of the last few years.

Alas, it’s been among the worst-performing asset *something-something* around — flat for half-a-decade, unremarkable in anything but its hype-bubble-and-subsequent collapse. Don't look at the chart this week.

“Institutions,” as a [magic incantation](https://x.com/joakimbook/status/2123798010174099756), hasn’t generated net new buyers (https://stacker.news/items/1506425), either.

Everything is already built, we have *all the tools*, we *desperately* need a better/freer/safer/fairer money etc… **yet, it’s crickets over here. Nobody wants this, nobody likes this.** The most successful thing to come out of Bitcoin is Tether, a literal freedom dollar to arbitrage government interest expenses and the third world's poor access to dollars. https://stacker.news/items/1453638

(also, a TOTAL “Guy in corner of party” meme situation: or, more Stoically and Big-Shorty: "[I guess when someone's wrong, they never… they never know how."](https://www.magicalquote.com/moviequotes/i-guess-when-someones-wrong-they-never/))

I devoted my professional life to writing/editing, two tasks that machines now do, not necessarily “better,” but good enough and *especially* fast enough and cheap enough, that it’s mostly a work of charity/patronage at this point https://stacker.news/items/1610192. (Also, in the age of [AI and infinite generation,](https://stacker.news/items/1449095) nobody cares about human-written/-created content — at least not enough to pay for it — so rents, “value-add,” are mostly entirely competed away.)

## At what point should I (or Jason) have known better?

I dunno. I legit can't point to a moment at which he (or I) should have made better/different choices.

And it's the story of every (failed) start-up or business: You sacrifice/take a chance to pursue what you believe in and what you thought was important — only to find that it doesn't work out, and then bad shit happens, and then you’re screwed. (Doesn't help that, in the meantime, the asset you devoted your life to stops working and collapses in value before your eyes...) At any point in your start-up's journey, **you gotta gauge the trajectory and if this recent dip is a low point that will pass, or the turning point for total collapse.**

You can't know that, and the extremely lucky/rich AI peeps (https://stacker.news/items/1617039, https://stacker.news/items/1617406, https://stacker.news/items/1617680) are the flip side of that process. *Every corpse on Everest was once an extremely motivated/convicted person*...

I’m coming to this from a similar angle, my regret or bad-fork-in-the-road happening 12-14 years ago ([https://stacker.news/items/879698?commentId=879742](https://stacker.news/items/879698?commentId=879742)) in going to university; maybe 8-9 years ago in not getting a bullshit-fiat job after university; maybe 6 years ago moving to the end of the world; maybe 5-ish [years](https://bitcoinmagazine.com/markets/asset-bubbles-covid-19-make-bitcoin-case) ago, pivoting my work so much into the Bitcoin world https://stacker.news/items/1078866

At what point should I have known better? Is this a mere blip, a lull before a wonderful rebound, *or* critically, the beginning of the total end?

Obviously, you can’t know that and so you make the best of the skills/knowledge/hunches you have… Mises’ human action, *we’re all speculators, all the time* etc. https://stacker.news/items/1556891

Somehow Jason raised over [4 million sats](https://mempool.space/address/bc1q3k2mfct7mersgh9mkz3f8nc7y336pe62nc009m) from his ask, the value of which, unfortunately, is melting away like that proverbial ice cube. So I guess the takeaway is: *quit what you’re doing and live off someone else’s charity*. @Solomonsatoshi was right ALL ALONG. Incredible.

***

Finally, fate and efficient markets have a sense of humor: I told y'alls I've been trying **Invity**, this new, hyped,  European fintech/stacking company. https://stacker.news/items/1586158 https://stacker.news/items/1604577. Setting aside the fees and the hidden spread, they *do* give you €50/purchase bonus with a DCA program.

So the other day I caught this *perfectly* iconic and ironic screenshot for how **there are no free lunches** and this little orange dream of ours is, uh, a neat little dream designed for capital destruction. Saylor (and Bailey!) know a thing or two about that. 

![](https://m.stacker.news/167530)

*I was* gonna end this with a snarky little Den remark to just zap me scudos instead... but gold's exchange rate is collapsing *alongside bitcoin's* in a horrible reverse-debasement trade, so I guess **we all just stay poor instead.**

I dunno, man. Maybe McDonald's is hiring.

items.title: How to use your first s9 / Why I bought a trunk-load of broken, out of date, s9s
items.text:
<sup>Skip to the very bottom for a tutorial on setting up your first s9 space heater... The bulk of this post is potentially mind-numbing storytelling.</sup>

# What's the coolest thing you've ever bought out of the back of a trunk?

I bought my first bitcoin mining machine on Amazon. It was an s9k. When it arrived, I discovered that I still needed to buy a power supply, an ethernet cable, and had to figure out what an IP address was. This was the level of knowledge I was coming from, and it honestly wasn't that long ago. This was the first and last time I bought any model of s9 from a non-trunk dealer.

My next purchase was a few years later. I had a gig in Lexington, KY that had a paid rehearsal the day before. I knew I was going to be in town for a bit, so I found someone selling miners on craigslist. He had four functioning s9is and one broken one. This guy was a real bitcoiner. I actually knew what an IP address was, but this dude had my head spinning with new terminology: system log, overclocking, tuning. The list goes on and on. Most significantly, he made it clear that even a guy like me can actually read and understand all those weird words and numbers in the machine's GUI (another new fun term for me at the time).

So early October, as part of my ongoing quest to totally bankrupt myself out of ideological obsession, I bought 18 more s9s. The natural next step was to drive about an hour in the middle of the night, meet a stranger at a lonely truck stop, and buy a bunch of broken shit out of his trunk.

![](https://m.stacker.news/167496)

![](https://m.stacker.news/167497)

![](https://m.stacker.news/167498)

"But for real," you might ask, "why?" Well, I wanted to fix them up and sell them to other bitcoiners as space heaters...out of an [idealogical obsession](https://hashratehearth.c54hometech.com/). My thoughts was, "I'm devoting so much energy to this, why not get a little cash for my time, recycle[^1] in the best sense of the word, and decentralize the network all at once?"

# The student becomes the teacher

Unlike the previous seller, this man, with whom I was parlaying at the aforementioned truck stop, was *not* a bitcoiner[^2]. When I said that I preferred to pay in bitcoin, he made it very clear that he had never made a bitcoin transaction in his life (off an exchange), and it turned out that this day wasn't going to be an exception. Ultimately, I was able to send bitcoin **onchain** to his CashApp, so it kinda/sorta worked out ok. The transaction didn't fully confirm until we both got home, which was a little awkward. I offered to wait there until the full three confirmations made the transaction appear in his app, but it was already late, and I think I impressed upon him that I was enough of an ideologue, and he didn't have a category for someone like me being a scammer. I am not sure I follow that logic, but to each his own.

So that said, this guy was, in fact, really smart. He had designed his own immersion rig, was a general inventor of sorts, and had been using the s9s to heat his house, while sending the mining revenue to an exchange. ...and he was a cat owner.

# When life gives you lemons, use child labor.

So the next morning, I organized my stash.

![](https://m.stacker.news/167500)

![](https://m.stacker.news/167501)

![](https://m.stacker.news/167503)

Then I did some dad stuff...

![](https://m.stacker.news/167502)

Then abdicated my pumpkin carving duties, and instead organized an antminer carving session:

![](https://m.stacker.news/167505)

![](https://m.stacker.news/167506)

![](https://m.stacker.news/167507)

![](https://m.stacker.news/167508)

![](https://m.stacker.news/167509)

![](https://m.stacker.news/167510)

These machines needed some love, mostly due to the cats. But they also got some other upgrades. For some people, I intend to include [propaganda](https://stacker.news/items/1600205). The selection is currently light, but expanding. For other, more practical uses come to mind. Here's a [boot heater](https://stacker.news/items/975661) prototype that I'm working on. Further down the line is this potpourri maker:

![](https://m.stacker.news/167515)

![](https://m.stacker.news/167516)

![](https://m.stacker.news/167517)

I may one day try to do something brave that involves food, like @RevHodl does. Alas, at this point, my skills aren't near his level and I'm not that confident that I can make a foodsafe product.

# Trunk or Treat?

The following night was trunk or treat. My childhood predates the days of trunk or treat. Apparently, in its early days, parents just passed out candy from the back of a sedan. With the rise of the non-sporting, non-utilitarian sports utility vehicle, it has apparently become more of pop-up a diorama competition with free candy as bribes for the judges. Given the recent purchase, I threw a bunch of the disassembled miners in the back, and my wife made our trunk a "haunted data center." Unfortunately, I forgot to get a picture of the actual trunk, but suffice to say, it was a mess of disassembled antminers and something that my wife called "batting," which made it look like a cloud.

![](https://m.stacker.news/167511)

Given that data centers were a hot item on the election in Ohio the following week, we got a fun range of responses.

# But is this all a LARP?

I was beginning to think so, but as it turns out, no! All of this sat by the wayside until yesterday. I decided to bring three of these guys out to the local meetup last night, and they flew out the Subaru like hotcakes!

![](https://m.stacker.news/167512)

I was kind of surprised, to be honest with you. Unlike myself, the recipients of these s9s got their first machines fully functioning, with "relatively" intuitive firmware, the PSU **and** all necessary cables included. I even gave away one piece of propaganda. I made some cash, they got a great price, and I'm available to all of them for questions.

# Speak of the devil

So what do you do with your first s9 recycled space heater, one might ask? It's quite simple.

1. Figure out how to get your sats. For an absolutely beginner, why not mine to Braiins's pool. It's KYC medium. They ask for your email address, but don't really verify it. So get an account at Braiins and click on "add miners." You're just going to be cutting and pasting from here. Also, have a lightning wallet ready to receive funds from this Braiins account.
2. Plug in the power and the ethernet. Optionally, buy a Vonets wifi bridge to free things up physically.
3. Find the machine's IP address. You can use a program like AngryIP for this. Type that IP address into a browser on any computer signed into the same network.
4. Figure out the password. Any machines that I sell uses the stock password settings. If it's the original Antminer firmware, that's root for the user and root for the password. For Braiins it's the same. For HiveOS it's root and root@. You can easily find others online.
5. In the GUI (graphical user interface), find your pool configuration and paste in the pool url from Braiins. Then in the username or workername line, put your account name from Braiins, followed by a dot, followed by whatever you want for your miner name. Put an x for password or leave it blank. Save, and wait a few minutes to see your miner show up in your Braiins account.
6. If you run your new space heater continuously, step 6 is taking those funds and buying a coffee about every two weeks from a shop that accepts lightning payments.
7. If you bought a machine from me, it should be underclocked to about 1000 watts. Underclocking means running the miner on purpose at a lower setting than it can handle. There are two good reasons to keep it that way. The first is your wiring. Pulling too much power through a circuit for hours on end is a fire hazard, and that goes for any space heater. At 1000 watts, the miner draws about 8.3 amps from a standard US 120-volt outlet. A typical 15-amp circuit shouldn’t carry more than about 12 amps continuously. That leaves room for a lamp and a laptop, but not a second space heater. The second is noise. Less power means slower fans, and slower fans mean a quieter machine. Chances are I also gave you quieter fans than the stock ones, but the lower setting still helps. So your action step number 7 is...don’t mess with the power. If you decide to ignore this step, the power setting is in the miner’s settings page. Before you change it, find out what else runs on that circuit and decide how much noise you can live with.

[^1]: upcycle? reuse?

[^2]: 100 sats to the first person to find the shitcoin miner that he snuck into the load (200 sats if you can do this and also convince me that you're not a bot). Circle it in any of the pics.

items.title: How turn Stacker News into Silk Road 3.0
items.text:
Stacker News is built around money. Money is integrated into almost every aspect of the platform. And yet Stacker News is not really used as a market (despite ~AGORA's commendable efforts). Most likely this is due to the cold start problem: getting a new online market off the ground is clearly very difficult. I believe one way of solving this cold start problem is by offering illegal items for sale.

But no one wants to go to jail. So here is a suggestion for how to mitigate the culpability of the sale of illegal items (I'm not sure if it really does mitigate it very much, though).

# Requirements:

1. end to end encrypted DMs
2. new post kind called `listing`

# How it could work

A seller creates a new `listing` post. `Listing` posts are different from other posts kinds in that the fee for commenting is the cost of the item listed and each comment is an end to end encrypted so that only the post creator and the comment create can read a particular comment.

When a stacker wants to buy a listed item, they reply with relevant delivery info

* For example, if the listing is for an illegal Stacker News hat, a stacker who is interested in buying such a hat would provide such info as a shipping address and color selection in the comment
* If the listing is a digital item, paying the fee to post a comment might result in an autoreply from the seller with a download link.

All the same rules about item ranking would apply to `listing` posts (zaps, downzaps, boosts).

# Bonus ideas

* **Review System** - Stacker News can verify a payment has been made. Therefore, only stackers who buy an item from a seller can be allowed to post a review which might - be displayed on the sellers' bio.
  **tor-only mode** - perhaps `listings` are only displayed if a user accesses Stacker News through a tor connection (unclear if there is a benefit to this).

# Flaws

The biggest flaw I can see is that if there are a bunch of `listings` for illegal drugs and other illegal things posted on Stacker News, the people running Stacker News may still be held responsible for the existence of those adds -- even if there is no evidence of sales (or said evidence is encrypted).

# Motivation

Selling and buying stuff with bitcoin is the original dream of Bitcoin:

> Commerce on the Internet has come to rely almost exclusively on financial institutions serving as trusted third parties to process electronic payments. While the system works well enough for most transactions, it still suffers from the inherent weaknesses of the trust based model. Completely non-reversible transactions are not really possible, since financial institutions cannot avoid mediating disputes. The cost of mediation increases transaction costs, limiting the minimum practical transaction size and cutting off the possibility for small casual transactions, and there is a broader cost in the loss of ability to make non-reversible payments for non-reversible services.

# How would you improve this system?

items.title: Total Chess Champ: Hans Narrowly Clinches 5th & Can the Stackers Find Mate-in-3?
items.text:
Hans *smooookey* Niemann lost a lot of games against Duda today -- BUT, by virtue of winning yesterday's set and then holding the draw in armageddon, he snatches the top spot in bracket 2 (thus 5th place overall)

Here's [one game he won, in the rapid segment](https://www.chess.com/events/2026-total-chess-world-championship-tour-pilot-knockout-bracket-2/02-02-06/Niemann_Hans_Moke-Duda_Jan_Krzysztof). In an interview afterwards, our beloved little media star/drama attractor said:

## "The knockout format is tremendously enjoyable"

> This is what chess should be: You should feel the tension and the stress at every single moment

Yeah, bro; *we know*. And we play crap chess online, not serious tournaments with serious prize money. *I can't imagine YOUR heart rate.* 

***

On move 11 of a fairly standard Sicilian defense (*lol* game review LITERALLY calls it "The Normal Line"), Duda couldn't figure out what to do or remember some prep, so spent 8 of his remaining 12 minutes doing, uh, nothing. Hans *immediately* pushed a pawn and tried squeezing Duda on the clock.

Pandemonium begins a few moves later, with a slight advantage for Hans (but with 8 *minutes* on the clock vs Duda's 40 seconds)

![](https://m.stacker.news/167598)

Duda apparently goes totally wrong with Rf3 where, after Be4 (which Hans finds), white can just *eat pawns* in the center (pawns around the queen are doubly pinned) with Bxd5 Hans doesn't find *exactly* that idea, but it develops along those lines anyway... first attacks the rook with Bg2: a *losing* move, but the refutation is to let the rook on h3 perish by attacking the bishop on g5 with your knight instead... good luck figuring that out with 28 seconds vs 5 minutes on the clock when you rook was *just* attacked on the previous move. 

Duda uno-reverses with the rook and attacks the bishop instead, and we get to the main course of pawn eating in the center:

![](https://m.stacker.news/167600)

**Bxd5**. Duda counterattacks the queen with Rb8; Hans *counter-counterattacks* by just moving his bishop out of the way: **take my queen, bro, I'll take yours WITH AN ATTACK ON YOUR BISHOP**

With both queens hanging, Duda says, *naaah, Imma SAAC THE ROOOOOK* instead...

![](https://m.stacker.news/167601)

...the idea being that after recapture, black has a check with the queen on a3, thinking he'll get out of his troubles. Down a queen, Hans says,

## That's so cool, Imma just gonna mate you instead

![](https://m.stacker.news/167602)

...in time trouble, Duda moves the king to f8 (engine shows another way out by blocking with the knight... but it's +8 and you're dying in a few moves ANYWAY; horizon effect), and it's *mate-in-three*. **Can the stackers find the right combo from here??**

![](https://m.stacker.news/167603)

items.title: Total Chess Championship: Magnus Saccing Queens for Shits and Giggles
items.text:
Been *totally* neglecting my coverage of the events in Budapest. (https://stacker.news/items/1617184). I've been busy... snow, IRL, beautiful weather, writing: you know the drill. Also... $ANT and the red-light therapy/meltdown in financial markets. Nobody is having a good time, etc https://stacker.news/items/1618180, https://stacker.news/items/1618301

but like, OMG... Magnus forfeiting/not showing up for classical games; then *not showing up for rapid games*. I understand nothing. Jeez. It's like the chess world equivalent of BIP-110... just a complete shitshow and waste of everyone's time: S-T-O-P--I-T!

***

In [one of the rapids](https://www.chess.com/events/2026-total-chess-world-championship-tour-pilot-knockout-bracket-5/02-02-05/Artemiev_Vladislav-Carlsen_Magnus) today between Magnus and Artemiev (fighting for, I believe, 17th place in the tournament, whatever), we got *this* juicy position:

![](https://m.stacker.news/167590)

## Can you, or can you *not* take that e4 pawn as black?

...Magnus goes for it. *takes-takes-takes-takes* and half of the minor pieces leave the board. *Here*, then, Artemiev plays the world's most natural move -- move the bishop to attack the queen, even if it may lose you a knight (the e8 rook behind is unprotected so whatevs):

![](https://m.stacker.news/167591)

Game Review had a little too much to drink, thinks it's a brilliant...*but you gotta sac your queen by playing bishop to f5 LOL.*

Point being you get the rook (on e4) *and* the knight on d4 (because the queen can't stay protecting it, or if she tries with Qc3, we just pin and with c5)

Magnus plays the more forcing version of that... SAAAACS THE QUEEN ON e1 -- which doesn't work because... *I don't even know why*. Computer says no:

![](https://m.stacker.news/167592)

+3 in that queen vs pieces endgame, Artemiev just made a draw. Down seven minutes on the clock against the GOAT, fine, maybe just take it instead of grinding it out, whatever.

Photo from last night:

Hahaha, look at how comfortable he is.

Who would’ve thought that the little cat abandoned in the parking lot would end up being so pampered by SN?

![](https://m.stacker.news/167546)

![](https://m.stacker.news/167547)

He has already received 2 doses of dewormer; the next one is due on Wednesday, and then another one 7 days after that third dose.

There are 5 days left in the treatment with the eye drops; by far the best way to do this is to wrap him in a sheet or blanket while one person holds him, and the other person applies the drops.

The issue with his/her loose stools is still giving me a headache. It has been a week since the treatment began; there was significant improvement during the first two days, but then things went back to how they were before. He/she has been given a dewormer, probiotics, and an antifungal, yet his/her stomach remains the same.

The subject of pet nutrition might seem simple, but it is actually quite complex. There is a great deal of conflicting information: some people fully endorse high-quality dry food though, of course, there are lower-quality options that contain more fillers (flours) than actual protein arguing that homemade diets may fail to provide all the essential nutrients a cat needs, such as taurine. Others, by contrast, advocate exclusively for homemade food, claiming that commercial dry or canned cat foods are actually harmful to cats.

Yesterday, I made a homemade pâté for him. I boiled a whole chicken though it didn’t include any giblets along with half a carrot. Once it cooled, I removed all the meat, discarded the bones, and blended the meat and carrot with a little of the water the chicken had been boiled in. He loved it and ate it with great enthusiasm; next time, I’ll buy some extra giblets, like liver and heart, to add to the mix.

![](https://m.stacker.news/167554)

![](https://m.stacker.news/167555)

His gastrointestinal issue needs to improve so that he can receive the remaining vaccine and subsequently be neutered.

items.title: How out of date is the Bitcoin network? - @schmidty
items.text:
@schmidty posted this snapshot of Bitcoin nodes that are running end of life versions versus those that are running still maintained versions:

![](https://m.stacker.news/167537)

And then he provided a little anlaysis of the state of the network:

---

I lined up Bitcoin Core's security advisories against a Bitnodes snapshot from this morning.

The short version:
- 59% of reachable nodes (about 12,800) are missing the October 27 fixes for two bugs that let peers exhaust a node's memory
- 16% (about 3,450) are on 28.x or older, without the fix for a high-severity crash
- About 500 on 24.x or older can be crashed by any peer with a few messages. 

Apart from the 28.x crash, no hashpower/mining is needed. Any peer that can connect to your node can execute these.

Today added one more. Bitcoin Core 31.3 and 30.5 shipped this morning alongside the disclosure of CVE-2026-117348 (medium, easily discoverable). A peer can freeze your node for over a dozen seconds at a time (~Raspberry Pi nodes, even longer), again and again, by spamming announcements for one orphan transaction. 

Nearly all of these crash, stall or slow down a node. None is a known way to steal coins. A stall is milder than a crash for one node, but it costs an attacker almost nothing to repeat. Someone who connects to every reachable node and stalls them all, over and over, degrades block and transaction relay for the whole network.

Below, I list what vulnerabilities each version is exposed to. Each version also has the bugs listed under the newer versions above it (sans a few that only exist in newer code). Today's bug, for example, starts at 29.0. Knots is counted by the Core version it is built on.

On 29.x, 30.x or 31.x, and not on 31.3 or 30.5? (12,004 nodes, 55%. 31.3 and 30.5 came out today.)
- A peer can freeze your node, over and over, by spamming announcements for one orphan transaction (CVE-2026-117348, medium).

Not on at least 32.1, 31.2, 30.4 or 29.5? (12,820 nodes, 59%)
- A malicious peer can make your node queue announcements for it forever, slowly eating memory (up to 2MB per hour per connection) until it runs out (CVE-2026-117349, medium).
- On macOS, Windows and BSD, a peer can run you out of memory with TCP urgent data (CVE-2026-117350, medium).

29.x (4,697 nodes, 21%; 8,146 or 37% on this line or older)
- A peer can stall your node for a few seconds at a time, as often as it likes, with crafted invalid transactions. That can delay block propagation (CVE-2025-46598, low).
- On 29.0 and 29.1, a peer can hold up your block processing for 10 minutes at a time with a tampered compact block (CVE-2025-62859, medium).
- On 29.0 and 29.1, miners can get stuck unable to build block templates after a reorg until restart (CVE-2025-62861, high).

28.x (1,370 nodes, 6%; 3,449 or 16% on this line or older)
- An attacker who mines a block can crash your node through a memory bug in script validation. Code execution is called unlikely but not ruled out (CVE-2024-52911, high).
- Every 28.x also has the stalls and memory bugs listed above, apart from today's orphan stall. That includes the compact block stall on all of 28.x, since its fix was never backported.
- 28.0 to 28.2 have the TRUC reorg bug.

25.1 to 27.x (662 nodes on 27.x, 601 on 26.x, 131 on 25.1 to 25.2; 6% together, 2,079 or 9.5% on these lines or older)
- Same as 28.x minus the TRUC bug. Nothing new has been disclosed for these lines yet. Medium and high issues fixed in 31.0 and 32.x stay under embargo until the older lines go end of life.

25.0 and older (685 nodes, 3%)
- A peer can delay your blocks about 10 minutes at a time by announcing and then withholding them (CVE-2024-52922, medium).

24.x and older (494 nodes, 2.3%)
- A single peer can crash you with a few crafted compact block messages (CVE-2024-35202, high).
- Mutated blocks can clear your download state and delay blocks (CVE-2024-52921, medium).
- Heavy transaction traffic can choke the node's ability to talk to peers (medium).

22.x and 23.x (183 nodes, 0.8%; 359 or 1.6% on these lines or older)
- A peer can crash the node by feeding it a long chain of low-difficulty headers. Building the chain costs a small fraction of mining one block, and it can be reused against every node (CVE-2019-25220, high).

0.21 and older (176 nodes, 0.8%)
- A peer can crash the node by spamming addresses (CVE-2024-52919, high).
- 0.20 adds a netsplit via timestamp manipulation and transaction censorship by a single peer.
- 0.15.0, 0.15.1 and 0.16.0 to 0.16.2 have the inflation bug (CVE-2018-17144).

How hard are these to pull off?
Most need no mining and no reorg, just a connection to the victim node. None of those require much skill to pull off, and an LLM will write the script from the advisory text.

Every version, including 32.1, has bugs nobody has found yet. But LLM-driven vulnerability scanning over the past year or so has been pointed almost entirely at current code, and I'm not aware of anyone running it against old releases. Old releases contain code that has since been rewritten or removed, so a bug that lives only there has never been through that scanning and has no fix coming. The reverse is also true. A bug introduced in newer code is not in the old releases, and today's CVE is an example, since a 28.x node does not have it. Version diversity limits the blast radius of an undiscovered bug in 32.x. The difference is that the bugs in old versions are known, and anyone who can connect to the node can trigger a bunch of these.

What about Knots? Knots is a Core fork, so the above applies by the Core version it is built on, in theory.

If you run a node, check your version. 32.1, 31.3 and 30.5 are the releases with every published fix.

Will the bulls show up for one day or do the bears sweep the week 5 to 0?

🟩 or 🟥?

items.title: The Resolution Hypothesis
items.text:
[they also have a nice website](https://lineshogan.github.io/resolution-hypothesis/)

***

> Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks.
>
> We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models, we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level, helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level, typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck.
>
> Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.

---

The problem of attributing improvements to the change or `rand()` is real. I got stuck last week trying to do some skill improvements (without LLM-as-a-judge even!) 

But, in the tooling section, I found that they use [`Trace2Skill`](https://github.com/Qwen-Applications/Trace2Skill)[<sup>(paper)</sup>](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.25158) as the baseline for optimization, so I have hope again and plan to deploy that in my quest to hammer Kimi K3.1 (or GLM 5.3, since Dario is so scared of it) into being as good a bug hunter as Opus 5.5[^1]. Worth a shot, I think.

[^1]: I need to hedge against US models increasing sAfEtY even further. It really sucks when a bot tells you trustmebro on a bug on your own software and refuses to give you the fixtures that you need to verify the claim. This (knowing the fixture) is an essential function when you're writing code that aims to improve app security, so I need to not be vendor locked on this, or locked out by some half-honest `narabamative` doomerist regulation.

items.title: PC Necromancing
items.text:
The story isn't as sexy as the title, but I thought it was good eye-catcher. Basically, this is another dribble about bringing another zombie computer chassis back to life. I was at the local ReSTORE thrift the other week, just checking the place out for what was available or interesting. Basically, ReSTORE is a construction-focused thrift operation; those folks with too much material left over and unwilling to re-use it or re-sell can just donate the materials and resources, and the ReSTORE folks sell it for big discount. It's a good way to find a lot of free construction and renovation materials if you're flexible. Inventory includes everything from tiles to windows to furniture to plumbing and so on, but they do take a lot of other stuff too. As it turned out, that's where my zombie was sitting.

Just about finished making my rounds and getting a feel for the overall offerings, I end in the miscellaneous section. Buried in a bunch of wiring, wi-fi modems and printers there sits an old Dell Optiplex mid-tower (not the cheapo slim version), covered in dust. A quick scan tells me it's a Windows 7 era version, probably from before they started farming out the sandwich PCs to the office types. That might have some promise, but I have no way of looking inside because it's sealed up. So, after rummaging a bit more and finding about two dozen books for free (easy resell on Pangobooks or Mercari), I find a staffer and ask if I can borrow their screwdriver to open the lid and see inside. Took a bit for him to find a Phillips (I should have just had one in my pocket but my work building security gets fussy with even spoons much less anything metal that you could poke something with), but eventually he comes back. Two screws off and the lid removed and I find a rabbit's nest of dust. However, buried deep inside is clearly four DDR chipsets, a CPU with a cooler on it, and a fatty hard drive along with the motherboard. Basically, some IT shop probably cleared the unit, deleted data and had this sitting for reallocation until it got timed out. So they out-cycled it and the PC found it's way to a thrift without ever being opened or gone through.

Dragging this find home, the first job was to just open up and see what I actually had. After some serious air-blowing and dustmigating (made up word) I finally was able to see the insides. Inventory: 1 Pentium dual-core CPU chip with matching cooler fan, 1 intel-format motherboard, 4 DDR 3 chips, but oddly 6GB in total (it ended up being a 2GB x 2 and 1GB x 2, weird), a clean 450W PSU, and a 650gb drive in decent condition. Tried to boot the machine on its own, but the results made it obvious why the machine got tossed - video wasn't working. After isolating the problem, the motherboard was toast and a tosser. However, for $20, everything was in working order.

So, since I couldn't bring the zombie back to life as-is, it got cannibalized into another zombie I now had available (ended up with a spare after cannabilizing the good stuff from that spare into a DDR5 modern machine I built separately). Now, popping the drive into an AMD-format motherboard it was a "simple" matter of sticking a new linux OS on it (Debian) and getting some value back. Oh dear, this is where the fund started. Turns out my spare didn't have a wi-fi modem built-in or a dongle, so Debian loaded with only the stripped-down CLI version. Now I had to figure out how to get it Internet in the garage. Tried it again with a dongle, but for some reason the install didn't want to cooperate after that, probably sensing network management at a foobar level was already loaded. So, now I had to plan B. Piggyback.

I had a few other PCs in the garage already wired and running. So, after digging around, I find a suitable patch cable and connect the ethernet of the zombie/cannibal package to a working PC and run off it's internet. Of course, in Linux, nothing is ever plug and play. Then I had to spend 30 minutes getting the host PC to recognize the connection, allow it's traffic and give the zombie/cannibal an IP address that would stick and be remembered. Once that defaults were defined, sticking and reliable with some minor work in Nano editor and bash, I had a working internet connection on the zombie/cannibal. Add in another hour loading my suite of standard apps via APT pulls, and finally getting GNOME set up properly, zombie/cannibal is purring like a kitten. 

The whole resurrection was a bit of a 4-hour pain, but for me these jaunts are a bit like an archaeology project getting old tech to work again in viable form. Linux is great for that, but it takes some technical know-how beyond just plug and play. As for the rest of the parts, I have a spare intel-CPU now to sell as well as some old DDR3 chips someone might need, so my guess is I'll probably double my initial $20 spend by the time everything is done.

items.title: Democrat-Touted Grocery Co-Op Collapses After 16 Months
items.text:
> Prairie Food Co-op, a member-owned grocery store in Lombard, Illinois, backed by about $1.56 million in state and federal grants, is winding down store operations 16 months after it opened, its board told owners on Nov. 11.
>
> The store opened in July 2025 in the Eastgate Shopping Center, selling sustainable, locally and regionally sourced food. An owner survey, the board wrote, "made clear that the store was not meeting many shoppers' needs, particularly around produce selection, pricing, and the availability of conventional grocery options" alongside its natural and organic lines.
>
> The bigger fixes, a produce reset and more conventional brands, stalled because the co-op couldn't line up responsive conventional suppliers. The store also faced "substantial rent obligations, including deferred and unpaid rent," and needed a gross margin of about 35% that its own advisers said would be hard to reach while cutting prices.

How it started:

![](https://m.stacker.news/167513)

How it's going:

![](https://m.stacker.news/167514)


I remember learning an important lesson about non-profits in grad school:

In competitive markets, for-profit companies are already operating as efficiently as they can on razor-thin margins.  Therefore, non-profits' room to behave differently than for-profits is limited by their ability to fundraise off donations.  If they aren't able to do that significantly, then they're going to be forced to behave similarly to for-profits, or else shutter.

Not saying this grocery store was a non-profit, but the point is that it's really difficult to improve on the efficiency of existing businesses in a competitive marketplace.  Good intentions usually isn't enough.

items.title: A Tiny Defense Stock That Could Soar if China Cuts Off America?
items.text:
This stock newsletter promotion is from Matt McCall of Early Opportunities. He's calling it the "Edison Prophecy", claiming one small American company could become critical to US military technology. The mystery stock is LightPath Technologies (LPTH).

The argument is interesting. Military drones and thermal cameras often depend on germanium, a material heavily controlled by China. LightPath develops alternatives that could reduce that dependence and the numbers actually look promising:

- Revenue grew 38% last quarter to $20.8 million.
- Order backlog reached a record $132.9 million.
- The Pentagon funded further development of its germanium alternatives.

But there's a catch, LightPath still lost $1.7 million last quarter and expanding production requires substantial investment. McCall is also emphasizing November 27, when China's suspension of certain export restrictions expires. But that doesn't mean China will automatically cut off supplies that day.

He also mentions Blue Moon Metals (BMM), which owns a former US germanium mine but hasn't restarted commercial production. I think the defense supply-chain opportunity is real. I'm less convinced it guarantees a stock market winner.

Would you invest in LPTH now, or wait for profitability?
